text: (b) You have also carried out fieldwork and research into a question about Diverse Places. Assess how far your conclusions answered the question posed in the geographical investigation. (9) Geographical enquiry question:
msText: Question Assess how far your conclusions answered the question posed in the geographical number investigation. Answer 6(b) AO3 (9 marks) Marking instructions Markers must apply the descriptors in line with the general marking guidance and the qualities outlined in the levels-based mark scheme below. No marks for stating the enquiry question, but this should be used as the context for the answer. Indicative content guidance Content depends on the student’s enquiry question, and the conclusions drawn. Assessment could include the following: • The ideas suggested in the specification are: • evaluation of areas that have potential for improvement • attitudes towards geo-demographic change • extent of deprivation in an area. • Conclusions could include the response to the question, including the findings from primary and secondary data. Comments about the use of statistical and presentation methods might also be relevant. • The question or hypothesis may have been based on a theory or model, or be based on a comparison of two places, or change along a transect. • Assessment about how far the question was answered might consider the scale of the investigation. For example, how far the sampling was representative of the range of views, or whether a large enough range of places was surveyed. • Another route might be to criticise the data collection methods themselves, and to suggest the impacts this had on the conclusions. • Suggestions of ways the investigation might have been improved would also be relevant. • If the question was not answered in full, then the assessment of the accuracy or reliability of the data obtained might be questioned. Accept any other appropriate response. Do not accept fieldwork contexts for Glaciation or Coasts. Level Mark Descriptor 0 No rewardable material. • Shows evidence that fieldwork investigation skills used may not have Level 1 1–3 been fully appropriate or effective for the investigation of the geographical questions/issue. (AO3) • Considers the fieldwork investigation process/data/evidence, with limited relevant connections and/or judgements. (AO3) • Argument about the investigation is simplistic and/or generic. (AO3) • Shows evidence that fieldwork investigation skills used were largely Level 2 4–6 appropriate and effective for the investigation of the geographical questions/issue. (AO3) • Critically considers the fieldwork investigation process/data/evidence in order to make some relevant connections and valid judgements. (AO3) • Argument about the investigation may have unbalanced consideration of factors, but is mostly coherent. (AO3) • Shows evidence that fieldwork investigation skills used were Level 3 7–9 appropriate and effective for the investigation of the geographical questions/issue. (AO3) • Critically considers the fieldwork investigation process/data/evidence in order to make relevant connections and judgements that are supported by evidence. (AO3) • Argument about the investigation includes balanced consideration of factors and is fully developed and coherent. (AO3)
erText: This year’s fieldwork question asked candidates to assess how far their conclusion answered the question they had posed at the start of their investigation. There were fewer L3 answers than in previous years. The mean and the modal mark were both 4. There was detailed description of findings from fieldwork, with comments about the methods used, and where and why these were used to investigate the question. However, many missed the focus of the question about how far their conclusion(s) answered the question. Most were able to offer some criticism of their methods and how these might affect their conclusions. Most of the assessment was at the end of the answer or each paragraph and was usually a comment of whether it did help or not. There wasn't much weighing up of 'how far', just a brief comment of it either did, did mostly or did not. The highest-level students presented their findings and developed this to talk critically about their methods/data used to come to this conclusion, and the top students provided some suggestions for improvements to the approach used. Stratford, London was often used as the focus for fieldwork in the answers seen. This question was well answered by most, as long as they gave themselves enough time to complete it. The difference across the responses was based on the range of points and detail as well as the evaluation. The majority of answers did show balance. All responses that had some degree of length could identify benefits and costs for both migrants and their families. In this way there was some implicit evaluation and often summary sentences at the end of each section. Most answers were focused on the resource which was generally well used. Answers that relied heavily on quotes or lifts from the resources often stayed in level 2, but there were also some that looked at the benefits for both sides and weighing these against possible negatives. Some up-to-date knowledge about the Windrush generation’s problems with the right-to-stay that is ongoing at the moment were discussed along with the effects on specific groups. Most conclusions that were not rushed gave a careful weighing of the relative importance of the benefits of international migration for migrants and their families. The best responses also considered the extent. Some sat on the fence and said there were benefits and costs for each group, and this tended to hold back their answer to level 3. Evaluation was usually a sentence at the end of each section or a paragraph at the end, but these were not particularly well developed. with its registered office at 80 Strand, London, WC2R 0RL, United Kingdom

text: 7 Study Figures 7a, 7b, 7c and 7d in the Resource Booklet. Evaluate the extent to which international migration brings benefits for both migrants and their families in Kingston, Jamaica. (16)
msText: Question Evaluate the extent to which international migration benefits for both migrants and their number families in Kingston Jamaica. Answer 7 AO1 (4 marks)/AO2 (12 marks) Marking instructions Markers must apply the descriptors in line with the general marking guidance and the qualities outlined in the levels-based mark scheme below. Responses that demonstrate only AO1 without any AO2 should be awarded marks as follows: • Level 1 AO1 performance: 1 mark • Level 2 AO1 performance: 2 marks • Level 3 AO1 performance: 3 marks • Level 4 AO1 performance: 4 marks Indicative content guidance The indicative content below is not prescriptive and candidates are not required to include all of it. Other relevant material not suggested below must also be credited. Relevant points may include: AO1 • The scale and pace of economic migration has increased as the world has become more interconnected, creating consequences for people. • International migration has increased in global hub cities and regions, deepening interdependence between regions. • Migration has economic, social, political and environmental costs and benefits for both host and source locations. • Culture and society change when significant international migration flows occur between the UK and former colonies. • Past and present connections have shaped places, leading to continuity and change. Places can be represented through different images and statistics. • People view their living spaces and cultural and demographic issues in different ways. AO2 Benefits to migrants and families Economic benefits • International emigration allows remittances to be sent home, enabling improved quality of life for family members. Money can be used to invest in local businesses, generating employment. • 40% of the poorest families rely on this additional income to support their livelihoods including basic necessities and improvements to housing. • Remittances make up about 23% of Jamaica’s GDP, which could help reduce reliance on government welfare for the poorest, enabling investment in other priorities. • Kingston is attracting migrants from overseas and the majority are well-qualified, contributing skills and spending to the local economy. • Some migrants return from lives overseas, bringing funds to invest and skills learned to benefit Kingston families, businesses and communities. • It may be possible for Kingston residents to obtain loans for their own businesses and houses as the remittances guarantee repayment. Social benefits • Older returning migrants volunteer in local community hubs to provide services, e.g. for barrel children who lack support from parents who have migrated themselves. • Children and young people can afford to attend university as parents earn more overseas. • Investment in improved water/sewage, healthier lifestyles, proper healthcare, and greater educational attainment make massive differences in life experience for those who receive them. • However, these highly educated young people may migrate themselves once qualified (brain drain), so gains for Kingston from an educated work force may not occur. • Migration has produced a community of diverse cultures. Problems caused by migration, which could form part of the evaluation Economic • Dependency on remittances can deter communities from self-reliance and hold people back from participating in the labour force. Families become over-reliant on handouts. • Over-reliance on remittances may create problems if they end. Social • Inequality of access to remittances may create resentment within a community between those who have and do not have relatives abroad. • Children may lack a strong relationship with their parents if they do not return home for year, leading to depression and isolation, especially if elderly relatives in Kingston become ill or die. • Elderly people in Kingston may lose both children and then grandchildren to migration, and lack support in their old age. • Children/teenagers without strong family support may be drawn into gangs, drugs and abuse. • Migrants who are deported back to Kingston from overseas may lack the support networks to provide them with the support they need, so they become a burden on the local community. Overall evaluation is likely to conclude that there are many economic and social benefits but socially, children suffer from weak relationships with parents, and elderly people may be neglected. Allow reference to both Kingston and Jamaica. Comparison with other places studied may be included. Level Mark Descriptor 0 No rewardable material. • Demonstrates isolated elements of geographical knowledge and Level 1 1–4 understanding, some of which may be inaccurate or irrelevant. (AO1) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas, making limited and rarely logical connections/relationships, to produce an interpretation with limited relevance and/or support. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to produce an unsupported or generic conclusion, drawn from an argument that is unbalanced or lacks coherence. (AO2) • Limited synthesis of geographical ideas from across the course of study. (AO2) • Demonstrates geographical knowledge and understanding, which is Level 2 5–8 occasionally relevant and may include some inaccuracies. (AO1) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas with limited but logical connections/relationships to produce a partial interpretation that is supported by some evidence but has limited coherence. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to come to a conclusion, partially supported by an unbalanced argument with limited coherence. (AO2) • Argument partially synthesises some geographical ideas from across the course of study, but lacks meaningful connections. (AO2) • Demonstrates geographical knowledge and understanding, which is mostly Level 3 9–12 relevant and accurate. (AO1) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to find some logical and relevant connections/relationships to produce a partial but coherent interpretation that is supported by some evidence. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to come to a conclusion, largely supported by an argument that may be unbalanced or partially coherent. question: 1(a)
mistakes: Movement of people across a national border to live in another country
vague answers or confusing it with internal migration within a country scored nothing
text: (a) Define the term ‘international migration’. (1)
msText: Question Define the term ‘international migration’. Mark number Answer 1(a) AO1 (1 mark) (1) Award 1 mark for correct answer: • Movement of people across a national border (1) • Any person who has changed his or her country of residence (1) • People who cross state boundaries and stay in the host state for some minimum length of time (1). • Movement from one country/nation to another (1). Accept any other appropriate response.
erText: The vast majority were able to score 1 mark here, with the most commonly seen answers being 'across borders' or 'between countries’ or something similar. Those who did not score the mark tended to make vague statements without reference to borders/other countries or confused it with intranational or internal migration and talked about movement within a country. Brevity was possible for this 1-mark question, and most scored the mark with responses of a few words.

skills.text: Dispersion: range, interquartile range, standard deviation

a correct answer without working now scores both marks

question: 1(b)(ii)
mistakes: High HDI means high GDP per capita, education and incomes, attracting TNCs and enabling travel and internet use, so higher KOF scores (e.g. Switzerland 0.962 and 91)
quote data from Figure 1 for the third mark
avoid circular reasoning and a second reason
text: (b) Study Figure 1 below: Country HDI KOF Index (0 – low (0 – low level of globalisation 1 – high) 100 – high level of globalisation) Australia 0.951 80 Chile 0.855 76 Costa Rica 0.803 71 Egypt 0.731 66 Ireland 0.945 85 Lithuania 0.879 81 Mexico 0.758 73 Switzerland 0.962 91 Figure 1 Human Development Index (HDI) and KOF Index data for selected countries, 2023 (ii) Suggest one reason why countries with a high HDI often have a high level of globalisation, as indicated by the KOF Index. (3)
msText: Suggest one reason why countries with a high HDI often have a high level of Question Mark globalisation, as indicated by the KOF Index. number Answer 1(b)(ii) AO1 (2 marks)/AO2 (1 mark) (3) Award 1 mark for analysing the resource to identify one reason a high HDI is linked to high levels of globalisation, and a further 2 marks for expansion up to a maximum of 3 marks. • High HDI is associated with a high number of years schooling (e.g. Switzerland) (1) so the country has residents with the qualifications to attract TNCs (1) which specialize in banking so need high levels of financial skills (1). • High HDI tends to mean the country has a high GDP per capita (1) so the so TNCs are attracted to locate there (1) and this makes the country more ‘switched on’ and globalised (1). • Some residents in a country with a high HDI have high incomes so they can afford to travel more (1) as flights and cruises are expensive (1) and so they experience the food and customs of other cultures (1). • A country with a high HDI such as Switzerland or Australia has high incomes and wages (1) so international migrants are attracted (1) and bring their language/culture/ food to the country (1). • High HDI includes high life expectancy (1) which could be due to access to quality health care/modern technology (1) gained from scientific research shared globally (1). NB to score 3 marks, one mark MUST come from the data, or refer to HDI or KOF index or a country in the resource booklet. Accept any other appropriate response.
erText: This question required candidates to use the data provided to suggest one reason why countries with a high HDI often have a high level of globalisation, as indicated by the KOF Index. In other words, candidates needed to find a reason for the relationship and needed to refer to data from the resource in their answer. Where there was specific reference to the resource, many examples of maximum marks were seen. High HDI was usually linked to high GDP/development and to personal income, which then allowed travel for tourism or business, or else the use of smartphones and access to the internet. A number missed the third mark usually due to failing to refer to data or else gave a briefer response. A minority went round in circles saying high HDI is linked to globalisation because globalised countries have a high HDI. These 3-mark questions with a resource are found on 8GE01, 8GE02 and also on 9GE01 and 9GE02. Candidates need to remember to refer directly to the resource in order to score all the available marks. Some started a separate second reason which could not be credited as the question asks for one reason. Centres are advised to practise these ‘chains of 3’ marks as a classroom activity. One student could identify a reason, and a second and then a third student could build on their answer, perhaps each beginning with the word ‘because’. This skill is useful for the 3- and 4-mark questions on all GCE papers, so it is well worth developing. The 4-mark questions do not have a resource.

question: 1(c)
mistakes: Lower or removed tariffs and quotas make trade cheaper
access to larger markets creates jobs
specialisation by comparative advantage
repeating the same expansion twice capped answers at 3 marks
msText: Question Explain two reasons why national governments promote free trade blocs. number Answer 1(c) AO1 (4 marks) For each way, award 1 mark for a reason national governments join trade blocs, and a further 1 mark for expansion, up to a maximum 2 marks each. For example: • Trade bloc membership means that taxes /tariffs are removed or are lower (1) so businesses can trade more profitably /prices of imports/exports are cheaper (1). • Trade bloc membership means a country can access a new market with more customers (1) so more jobs can be created to meet the demand(1). • Agreements to lower or remove taxes/tariffs (1) so goods/money/ services can move across borders more easily (1). • Trade blocs enable countries to specialize in producing goods and services where they have a comparative advantage (1) , leading to increased efficiency and competitiveness and profit, as borders can be crossed easily (1). • Trade blocs can help countries cooperate politically (1) and member countries can work together to achieve shared goals and support each other, as seen in the EU (1). Accept any other appropriate response.
erText: Again, this question was generally well answered, and 3 or 4 marks were frequently awarded. Candidates were asked to explain two reasons why national governments promote free trade blocs. Very few candidates scored 0 marks unless the question was unanswered. Most candidates could give two clear reasons and often expanded for the second mark in each case. Some repeated the expansion point in the second response, so only scored 3 marks. The main reasons given were reduction of tariffs and quotas and access to new markets. Some candidates did not really understand what a quota was and how it worked, and some were unable to explain how access to a new market benefited a country and therefore why a government might seek to join a trade bloc.

question: 1(d)
mistakes: Global shift moves manufacturing to places with cheap labour and weak environmental regulation (air and water pollution, biodiversity loss) v strict regulation in developed countries
deindustrialised places (Detroit, Redcar) have legacy problems
primary industry (Niger Delta oil) is off-topic
text: (d) Explain why there are variations in environmental problems caused by manufacturing. (6)
msText: Question Explain why there are variations in environmental problems caused by number manufacturing. Answer 1(d) AO1 (6 marks) Marking instructions Markers must apply the descriptors in line with the general marking guidance and the qualities outlined in the levels-based mark scheme below. Indicative content guidance The indicative content below is not prescriptive, and candidates are not required to include all of it. Other relevant material not suggested below must also be credited. Relevant points may include: • The environmental costs of global manufacturing are one of the results of the global shift of manufacturing to places where wages and land are at a lower cost. • There is likely to be loss of biodiversity, pollution of water and air and noise, and loss of farmland/forest in places where manufacturing is located. • Some countries may not have codes of practice, or these may not be enforced so TNCs can operate with impunity. National governments may fear the loss of the TNC as they bring employment and tax revenue, so they do not challenge the practices of the TNC. E.g. overuse of water by soft drinks manufacturers. • High levels of waste as a result of the manufacture of cheap goods, some of which has been shipped overseas for disposal, e.g. e-waste • Deindustrialised regions have contaminated land and devastated habitats which may take decades to recover as manufacturing has moved overseas. • Long journeys move goods via containerisation resulting in pollution along shipping lanes. Amongst the busiest are the Malacca Strait, English Channel and Suez Canal, as a result of the movement of goods from Asia to Europe and other destinations. • Some industries lead to higher environmental costs than others, such manufacturing plastics or dyeing material, so it likely that places that specialise in these will have more threats to biodiversity and contamination of water, air and land. • Allow a wide definition of manufacturing, including all types and recycling. Also allow generation of electricity/power to fuel the manufacturing. • For 6 marks, expect reason/s for the distribution of costs in different places, as well as a detailed account of reasons environmental costs occur. • The ‘variation of environmental costs’ may be in terms of the type of cost to the environment, as well as the locations where this is occurring. i.e. the variation does not have to be spatial. Accept any other appropriate response. Level Mark Descriptor 0 No rewardable material. • Demonstrates isolated elements of geographical knowledge and Level 1 1–2 understanding, some of which may be inaccurate or irrelevant. (AO1) • Understanding addresses a narrow range of geographical ideas, which lack detail. (AO1) • Demonstrates geographical knowledge and understanding, which is Level 2 3–4 mostly relevant and may include some inaccuracies. (AO1) • Understanding addresses a range of geographical ideas, which are not fully detailed and/or developed. (AO1) • Demonstrates accurate and relevant geographical knowledge and Level 3 5–6 understanding throughout. (AO1) • Understanding addresses a broad range of geographical ideas, which are detailed and fully developed. (AO1)
erText: In response to the question to explain why there are variations in environmental problems caused by manufacturing, most candidates scored 3 or 4 marks. Different approaches were acceptable, and there was an almost equal split between candidates who focused on variation in types of pollution and those who looked at the reasons for the current spatial distribution of manufacturing linked to global shift/cheap wages/ lack of regulations. The question provided the opportunity for candidates to use case study material to support their answers. Some strong case study material was seen, particularly contrasting UK regulation and monitoring of pollution with SE Asian countries and associated industries. Deindustrialisation answers often mentioned Detroit or Redcar. Some candidates strayed into writing about primary industry, particularly extraction of oil in the Niger Delta thus restricting their responses. Some more generalised answers about water and air pollution did not move out of level 1 unless they tied this to specific industries or locations. To achieve 5 or 6 marks, fuller knowledge of the reasons for the variation identified was required.

question: 1(e)

skills.text: Synoptic theme: Players

mistakes: TNCs spread globalisation via global production networks, outsourcing, offshoring and glocalisation (Apple, McDonald's, Disney)
weigh against transport and ICT (containerisation, Maersk, EasyJet), governments and IGOs
general cost-benefit essays on TNCs stayed in low Level 2
text: (e) Assess the role of transnational corporations (TNCs) in increasing global connections. (12)
msText: Assess the role of transnational corporations (TNCs) in increasing global connections. Question number Answer 1(e) AO1 (3 marks)/AO2 (9 marks) Marking instructions Markers must apply the descriptors in line with the general marking guidance and the qualities outlined in the levels-based mark scheme below. Responses that demonstrate only AO1 without any AO2 should be awarded marks as follows: • Level 1 AO1 performance: 1 mark • Level 2 AO1 performance: 2 marks • Level 3 AO1 performance: 3 marks. Indicative content guidance The indicative content below is not prescriptive, and candidates are not required to include all of it. Other relevant material not suggested below must also be credited. Relevant points may include: AO1 • TNCs are important in globalisation as they contribute to its spread (through global production networks, glocalisation and the development of new markets). • They also take advantage of economic liberalisation through outsourcing and off shoring. • TNCs have enabled cultural diffusion to occur through tourism and migration, and through social media. AO2 • Global production networks including complex supply chains have grown in length and in frequency of use in the 20th and 21st century, enabling TNCs to produce goods globally and transport them to markets. TNCs also build and operate these supply chains themselves (Airbus, Easyjet, Maersk, underwater cable companies). • TNCs are driven by profit, which is a powerful motivator both for both privately- owned (Apple, McDonalds, and state-owned TNCs including Sinopec), so any actions that enable them to produce cheaply and sell to as wide a market as possible will be attractive. • TNC wages enable local people employed or those who supply raw materials and goods to benefit through increased incomes. These people may be enabled to be more globalised as they can afford mobiles, internet connectivity and can afford to travel. • Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) by TNCs leads to economic links, but these may become cultural too, as cultural traits are exchanged alongside flows of money and commodities. Some local places may become highly connected e.g. export processing zones so globalisation is speeded up here ahead of the rest of country. • TNCs spread culture making the world more connected through film, food, social media, games for example. • TNCs, especially technology companies, have enormous power on account of their investments and the ideas and cultures that spread via different forms of trade, including music, language, food and clothing, social media, tourism. • TNCs operate where they can, so their role is controlled by the rules imposed by national governments. Governments may allow TNC investment (e.g. China’s Open Door Policy in 1978, which set up special economic zones) but they also make decisions to join (8 countries currently waiting to join the EU) or leave (UK in 2016) a trade bloc, or to limit the export of profits. These actions may speed up or hold back the contribution TNCs can make to globalisation in certain places and time periods. • National investment rules and laws allow TNCs to deploy (or not) financial strategies such as mergers and acquisitions and joint ventures. • TNCs need to repatriate their profits for shareholders, and some follow tax avoidance strategies, which limit the wealth shared with local communities. Assessment: • TNCs make an enormous contribution to globalisation through connecting the world via supply chains, as well as providing the technology and the social media networks to make deeper links. • Other factors are also crucial, particularly the role of national governments to encourage or prohibit the actions of TNCs. • TNCs could not make the world more connected without developments in technology, particularly the internet and transport systems. Level Mark Descriptor 0 No rewardable material. • Demonstrates isolated elements of geographical knowledge and Level 1 1–4 understanding, some of which may be inaccurate or irrelevant. (AO1) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas, making limited logical connections/relationships. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to produce an interpretation with limited relevance and/or support. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to make unsupported or generic judgements about the significance of few factors, leading to an argument is unbalanced or lacks coherence. (AO2) • Demonstrates geographical knowledge and understanding, which is Level 2 5–8 mostly relevant and may include some inaccuracies. (AO1) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas logically, making some relevant connections/relationships. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to produce a partial but coherent interpretation that is mostly relevant and supported by evidence. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to make judgements about the significance of some factors, to produce an argument that may be unbalanced or partially coherent. (AO2) • Demonstrates accurate and relevant geographical knowledge and Level 3 9–12 understanding throughout. (AO1) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas logically, making relevant connections/relationships. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to produce a full and coherent interpretation that is relevant and supported by evidence. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to make supported judgements about the significance of factors throughout the response, leading to a balanced and coherent argument. (AO2)
erText: This essay differentiated well, and there were good essays seen when candidates focused on the question which asked them to assess the role of transnational corporations (TNCs) in increasing global connections. A number wrote general essays about the costs and benefits of TNCs which tended to score low level 2 marks if there was a little exemplification. Many candidates showed good knowledge and understanding from both AO1 and AO2 sections of the mark scheme. There was frequent reference to major TNCs such as Apple, Dyson and McDonalds for support. Candidates made links to different sectors of industry for example explaining about outsourcing and offshoring and the reasons for it. As this was a ‘role of’ question, other factors which increase global connections were explored by candidates. There was some difference in what the candidates thought of as 'other factors’. Some referred to the travel and communication TNCs such as EasyJet and Apple, or to containerisation and Maersk. Stronger candidates then made judgments about the global connections facilitated by these TNCs to enable other businesses to develop their own connections through tourism or outsourcing. Some discussed the role of TNCs in building cultural connections, for example Disney adaptations to local characteristics and explained the ways McDonald's glocalises it food offers to meet local demand. Stronger candidates discussed SEZs, trade blocs and government censorship (North Korea) as 'others'. However, one of the main differences in candidates' responses was the degree to which they addressed the command word ‘assess’. Some, less developed answers explained the pros and cons of TNCs or gave a simple one-line judgement at the end, which limited progress up the mark levels.

question: 2(a)
mistakes: Answer B (quaternary): knowledge-based research and development
tertiary is a service sector
text: (a) Identify the term for a knowledge-based research and development business. (1) A Primary B Quaternary C Secondary D Tertiary
msText: Question Identify the term for a knowledge-based research and development business. Mark number Answer 2(a) AO1 (1 mark) (1) B Quaternary is correct as knowledge-based and research and development are key features of this sector of the economy. A Primary is not a correct category for this business C Secondary is not a correct category for this business D Tertiary is a broad category but is not appropriate for this employment type as there is no element of service included
erText: Most were able to identify the term for a knowledge-based research and development business as ‘quaternary’.

question: 2(b)(i)

skills.text: Percentages, ratios and rates of change

mistakes: a correct answer without working scores both marks
text: (b) Study Figure 2a in the Resource Booklet. (i) Calculate the percentage (%) of the total number of people in the UK aged 16–64 who are full-time workers. You must show your working. Give your answer to two decimal places. (2) ..............................................................%
msText: Question Mark Calculate the percentage (%) of the total number of people in the UK aged 16–64 number who are full-time workers. Answer 2(b)(i) AO3 (2 marks) (1 +1) 24.12 ÷ 43.25 X100 (1) = 55.77 (to 2DP) (1) Please note that a correct answer without working DOES score 2 marks. Pearson have changed this from previous years. Allow other routes to the correct answer
erText: The majority were able to select the appropriate data and calculate the percentage of the total number of people aged 16-64 who are full time workers correctly. Some covered the space available sheet with calculations, clearly spending too long on this question, and failing to find the correct answer. Centres are reminded to advise candidates to revise basic GCSE maths skills for Geography exams, using past papers as a guide. Thise who struggle with maths questions should glance at the question and avoid spending too long trying to answer it.

question: 2(b)(ii)

skills.text: Graphs and charts: read, interpret, complete or plot

mistakes: Use Figure 2b: 35.8% of those not working have poor health v 15% of workers
poor health limits ability to work, stress and mental health, discrimination by employers
quote data for the AO2 mark
text: (b) Study Figure 2a in the Resource Booklet. Study Figure 2b in the Resource Booklet. (ii) Suggest one way in which the health of a person in the UK may affect their economic activity. (3)
msText: Suggest one way in which the health of a person in the UK may affect their Question Mark economic activity. number Answer 2(b)(ii) AO1 (2 marks)/AO2 (1 mark) (3) Award 1 mark for analysing the resource to identify a way in which health affects economic activity and a further 2 marks for expansion, up to a maximum 3 marks. For example: • 35.8% of those not working have poor health (1) perhaps because they need to rest/go to appointments (1) and may not be able to get the time off from their job (1). • Some work is very stressful and causes mental health problems (1) so a person may not be able to work (1) to ensure they can look after their own well-being (1). • Those with poor health may suffer discrimination (1) because an employer may think they are unable to do the job effectively(1) so may not be appointed and may have to remain unemployed(1). • 85% of those in work have excellent, very good or good health, compared to 64.2% of those not working (1). Healthy people will have a wider range of job opportunities open to them (1) as they may be able to travel/stand /use machinery more than a person with poor health (1). Accept any other appropriate response. Allow one mark for use of data connected to a valid reason.
erText: This question examined a different part of the specification (4A.1b) about one way one way in which the health of a person in the UK may affect their economic activity. Data was provided, and again as in 1aiii, candidates were required to make reference to it in their answer. The majority of candidates took 'economic activity' as employment or earning potential whereas one or two regarded it as spending or level of purchasing power. Either of these were acceptable, and using data or making a comparison helped earned the AO2 mark interpreting the data. Answers that used the resource were able to show that candidates had an understanding of the impact poor health has on the ability to work. Some wrote in a way that gave the impression they were speaking from personal or family experience. Centres are encouraged to discuss these and other ideas from 4A.1b.

question: 2(c)
mistakes: Physical factors (coast, beaches, river crossing points, flat land, resources) shaping functions such as port, tourism, trade or mining
human factors and vague inland settings (e.g. Canary Wharf as finance) did not fit
'physical' is a word AS candidates struggle with
msText: Explain two ways in which physical factors influence the functions of one of your Question Mark chosen places. number Indicative content 2(c) AO1 (4 marks) (4) Award 1 mark for explanation of a way physical geography (including beaches, rivers, relief, location, weather has influenced the function of a place and a further 1 mark for expansion, up to 2 marks each. • Location of resources led to a focus on mining in the past e.g. coal, oil (1) so skills and infrastructure grew around this, which were left exposed when mining ended in the 1990s (1). • Shallow sea and sandy beach is suitable for tourism (1) so hotels and restaurants have been established and provide employment. (1) • Flat land / river crossing points allowed housing and trade to be established(1) so the city grew up around these and other firms located there, leading to specialization in finance and business /accessible for those who are less mobile. (1). • Only accept physical factors. Accept location as a physical factor, in terms of location in relation to other places. • No mark for naming the chosen place. Accept any place as their chosen place. • If no place is named, credit the answer according to the mark scheme • Accept any other appropriate response
erText: Most candidates could identify at least one physical factor and its influence on function. There was some repetition for the second factor, but candidates often linked it to a different function. Coastal locations, beaches and rivers frequently used and linked to trade, as was flat land for development or use as a port. Location as a factor was often vague but scored a mark. Problems arose when candidates did not focus on 'physical' factors and so their responses didn't fit the question. Some candidates seemed to use their fieldwork location which worked well on most occasions, but those that used more inland sites struggled, such as those who wrote about Brixton, Chelmsford, Stratford. Docklands worked if they focused on the river location for past trade or present residential buildings, but was not useful if they strayed into human factors for Canary Wharf. ‘Physical’ is a word AS candidates often struggle with, and centres are recommended to use it regularly in lessons to help develop confidence in concepts included and the ways physical geography shapes the places where people live and work.

question: 2(d)
mistakes: Migrant enclaves, foreign investment by TNCs, global shift causing deindustrialisation (e.g. Redcar), effects on the built environment
whole countries (China, UK) lacked detail and capped at 3 marks
use at least two different themes for Level 3
text: (d) Explain how international influences have shaped the characteristics of one of your chosen places. (6) Location of your chosen place:
msText: Question Explain how international influences have shaped the characteristics of one of your chosen number places. Answer 2(d) AO1 (6 marks) Marking instructions Markers must apply the descriptors in line with the general marking guidance and the qualities outlined in the levels-based mark scheme below. Indicative content guidance The indicative content below is not prescriptive and candidates are not required to include all of it. Other relevant material not suggested below must also be credited. Relevant points may include: • International influences could shape the characteristics of a place in terms of migrant enclaves which could be long standing or more recent. Migrants cluster for many reasons, with the benefits that they can develop systems of interpersonal relations to pass on knowledge, for example about employment, affordable housing, government assistance and helpful local networks or NGOs. This may be reflected in the built environment e.g. street signs/road names in a language appropriate to the community e.g. in Chinatown in London. • Places of worship (mosque/temple) and shops/services locate there to meet people’s needs. Culture may be reflected in the clothing/head coverings, in food and restaurants and in banks and other financial services, and in cultural festivals and ceremonies. • International influences in the economic characteristics could be in terms of factories that have moved overseas due the global shift in services/ manufacturing leaving high rates of unemployment, and a spiral of decline may lead to outmigration and other social issues. • Some locations have international TNC businesses or shops or providing employment or cultural influence to the community. • Food from elsewhere in the world is popular so takeaways dominate most high streets with fewer UK choices. • Deindustrialisation in parts of the UK due to global shift has led to a spiral of decline. • Tourists or sports supporters from overseas may provide economic opportunities, particularly in major tourist hotspots or when a major even takes place, e.g. Olympics or Euro football tournament. • Students and workers from overseas rent property. • Allow the idea that there have been minimal international influences on the economic or social characteristics of a place. The reasons for this would need to be developed in a relevant way to go out of level 1. If not linked to the chosen place, the answer is unlikely to go out of level 2. No mark for naming the chosen place and accept any place. Large places may be over- generalised. Reward specific detail. Allow a range of characteristics, including economic or social characteristics and the built environment, and appearance of the place. Accept any other appropriate response. Level Mark Descriptor 0 No rewardable material. • Demonstrates isolated elements of geographical knowledge and Level 1 1–2 understanding, some of which may be inaccurate or irrelevant. (AO1) • Understanding addresses a narrow range of geographical ideas, which lack detail. (AO1) • Demonstrates geographical knowledge and understanding, which is mostly Level 2 3–4 relevant and may include some inaccuracies. (AO1) • Understanding addresses a range of geographical ideas, which are not fully detailed and/or developed. (AO1) • Demonstrates accurate and relevant geographical knowledge and Level 3 5–6 understanding throughout. (AO1) • Understanding addresses a broad range of geographical ideas, which are detailed and fully developed. (AO1)
erText: This 6-mark question invited candidates to explain how international influences have shaped the characteristics of one of their chosen places. As with Q2c, candidates who opted to write about the whole of China or the UK lacked the specific detail to move up the level-based mark scheme, and 3 marks on this question tended to be the maximum mark. Choosing one area of eastern or southern China worked more successfully. Some answers were vague, and many lacked specific examples of the characteristics of the places they wrote about. Most answers focused on migration of people and/or businesses moving in, and some looked at deindustrialisation due to global shift of manufacturing. Redcar was used effectively by some candidates. Some potentially good answers were limited by generalities, and support would have easily raised the quality of the responses. To gain level 3 marks, it is recommended candidates use at least two different themes, for example migration of people as well as the effects on the built environment (mosques, restaurants, TNCs, road signs, language and culture) to demonstrate the ‘broad range of geographical ideas’ required.

question: 2(e)

skills.text: Synoptic theme: Attitudes and actions
Synoptic theme: Players

mistakes: Stakeholders (local and national government, developers, residents, businesses) with contrasting priorities, e.g. Stratford Olympic Park and Clay Lane residents, Heathrow expansion

text: (e) Assess why conflicts may occur between stakeholders involved in managing regeneration. (12)
msText: Assess why conflicts may occur between stakeholders involved in managing regeneration. Question number Answer 2(e) AO1 (3 marks)/AO2 (9 marks) Marking instructions Markers must apply the descriptors in line with the general marking guidance and the qualities outlined in the levels-based mark scheme below. Responses that demonstrate only AO1 without any AO2 should be awarded marks as follows: • Level 1 AO1 performance: 1 mark • Level 2 AO1 performance: 2 marks • Level 3 AO1 performance: 3 marks. Indicative content guidance The indicative content below is not prescriptive and candidates are not required to include all of it. Other relevant material not suggested below must also be credited. Relevant points may include: AO1 • Economic and social inequalities change stakeholders’ perceptions of an area and how both the need for regeneration and its success are regarded. • Regeneration may change the lived experience, perceptions, and attachments of groups of people/ stakeholders to their places, and this varies according to demographic factors and length of residence. • Stakeholders include local residents and business people, government (local and national), environmentalists. • A spiral of decline triggered by economic restructuring has occurred in some places, which has increased deprivation. • Decisions and judgements about managing regeneration are often contested, as stakeholders or groups weigh economic, social, demographic and environmental priorities by their own perceptions of the image and reality of the place. AO2 • Views about regeneration are different for each location, and each stakeholder or group will have their own perception, so conflict may occur where opinions are different. • Local and national governments have key roles in managing regeneration and their priorities are wide ranging. They might hope for a reduction inequality and improvements in terms of the built environment, but there might be conflicts over financial costs in terms of generating enough funding and staying within budget. For example, the recent Aviva Studio regeneration of the Granada Studios in Manchester went over budget, but was able to find private funding from Aviva, an insurance company. • Local residents might lack power in managing regeneration but will have strong views, for example they might welcome new housing and an improved built environment with safer streets, but conflict might occur over the limited affordability of housing for local people, or congestion and pollution brought by more visitors. • Businesses might welcome new contracts or customers, but they may experience costs through delays and disruption if the construction period is delayed (Aviva has taken over 9 years). Judgements will depend on the places and groups of people chosen and are likely to be partial and tentative given the complex nature of perceptions and time scales. For Level 3 expect discussion about management as well as reasons for conflict. Accept any other appropriate response Level Mark Descriptor 0 No rewardable material. • Demonstrates isolated elements of geographical knowledge and Level 1 1–4 understanding, some of which may be inaccurate or irrelevant. (AO1) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas, making limited logical connections/relationships. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to produce an interpretation with limited relevance and/or support. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to make unsupported or generic judgements about the significance of few factors, leading to an argument is unbalanced or lacks coherence. (AO2) • Demonstrates geographical knowledge and understanding, which is mostly Level 2 5–8 relevant and may include some inaccuracies. (AO1) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas logically, making some relevant connections/relationships. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to produce a partial but coherent interpretation that is mostly relevant and supported by evidence. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to make judgements about the significance of some factors, to produce an argument that may be unbalanced or partially coherent. (AO2) • Demonstrates accurate and relevant geographical knowledge and Level 3 9–12 understanding throughout. (AO1) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas logically, making relevant connections/relationships. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to produce a full and coherent interpretation that is relevant and supported by evidence. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to make supported judgements about the significance of factors throughout the response, leading to a balanced and coherent argument. (AO2)
erText: The 12-mark question asked candidates to assess why conflicts may occur between stakeholders involved in managing regeneration. Most candidates demonstrated quite strong AO1 understanding, with most identifying a range of stakeholders and the different priorities they have. AO2 application of ideas was also evident using exemplars to develop and exemplify the reasons for the conflicts occurring. Candidates could identify stakeholders but often lacked specific detail either about the conflicts between them or detail regarding case studies. There were some good answers on the extension of Heathrow, and the most popular examples seen were the developments at Stratford including the London Olympics park and the conflict between developers and residents of Clay Lane etc. There were some good opposing arguments provided as to why some areas don’t have conflict and may be more successful if they are bottom-up projects. Many did not go on to assess or even mention management. This was why many answers went no higher than level 2 (8 marks).

msText: Question Explain two limitations of this data collection sheet. Mark number Answer 3(a) AO3 (4 marks) (2+2) Award 1 mark for a limitation and a further expansion mark up to a maximum of 2 marks for each limitation • There are no numbers used (1) so this makes it difficult to compare across categories/hard to collate the results (1). • The descriptors used are vague / not clear (1) so the person filling it in would be unsure as to how to score (1). • “OK” doesn’t mean anything and has no value (1) therefore doesn’t help with the assessment (1). • The survey sheet is subjective (1) with no guidance about how to allocate scores (1). • There are only three categories shown for each criteria (1) which could be quite limiting in terms of range for some areas (1). • The question / context asked is not shown (1), so it makes it difficult to know how to score (1). • There is no weighting used (1) so this survey assumes all categories are of equal importance which they may not be (1). • It is not fully completed with blank categories (1) therefore judgements unreliable (1). • In ‘Exterior appearance of shops’ category two words are circled (1) therefore can’t make mind up on decision (1). • Allow mark/s about where the data was collected, as this is recorded on the sheet. • There is no place to record the date or the time of the day (1) this is needed to make comparisons possible and to improve the reliability of the data collection (1). Accept any other appropriate response. Do not credit points about the frequency of the survey as the question asks about the data collection sheet itself.
erText: This two by two 4-mark question asked candidates to explain two limitations of this data collection sheet. Some responses require improvement, but most were able to score at least 3 of the 4 marks available. Many candidates gained maximum marks as they were able to identify and explain two clear limitations of the sheet. The subjective nature of qualitative data does not necessarily lead to invalid data. Much human geography fieldwork relies on such data! However, here the lack of a clear scale or guidance to interpret terms such as ‘Few’, ‘Quite a lot’ and ‘Lots’ were clear limitations discussed by some.

text: (b) Explain one reason why sample size is important when collecting primary fieldwork data. (3)
msText: Question Explain one reason why sample size is important when collecting primary Mark number fieldwork data Answer 3(b) AO3 (3 marks) (3) Award 1 mark for a reason and further expansion / development marks up to a maximum of 3 marks. • Suitable sample size in relation to population is a key part of fieldwork design (1) since a larger sample size will cover a wider range of the diversity of the whole population (1) which improves the reliability of any conclusions (1). • Resources are going to be limited when collecting fieldwork data (1) so there won’t be enough time (1) to survey all parts of an environment so people have to make allowances for the fact (1). • Sample size might be controlled by the number of students (1) so the fieldwork design needs to consider the optimum size in order to get reliability (1) which then makes analysis and conclusions more valid (1). • A larger sample size means the average values will be more accurate (1) because the outliers in data will be identified (1) as more of the range of possible values is included in the sample (1). Accept any other appropriate response.
erText: As with the previous question, this was generally well answered with candidates clearly understanding the need for a large enough sample size for accuracy, validity and accommodating anomalies. Simply stated, larger samples are more representative of the whole place or people being surveyed. Some were able to discuss the size of samples needed for statistical tests.

text: (d) You have also carried out fieldwork and research into a question about Regenerating Places. Assess the value of secondary data used at different stages of your geographical investigation. (9) Geographical enquiry question:
msText: Assess the value of secondary data used at different stages of your geographical Question investigation. number Answer 3(d) AO3 (9 marks) Marking instructions Markers must apply the descriptors in line with the general marking guidance and the qualities outlined in the levels-based mark scheme below. Indicative content guidance Please remember that the descriptor provides guidance as to the appropriate level. Bullet points covering the indicative content do not translate directly into marks. . Content will depend on a student’s choice of geographical enquiry question. • Secondary data helps in understanding/ confirming an idea for investigation. • It could be used in planning, drawing up enquiry questions/hypotheses or in interpreting the results. • It also helps in planning safe and suitable locations for primary data collection, and helps carry out a risk assessment (e.g. weather forecast). • Secondary data may help interpret the primary data. • Expect details on secondary data used and its source, which could be assessed for the contribution to the investigation/ question. • Large scale surveys such as a census or ONS data are more representative than any primary data survey carried out in person, and comparisons with previous data may be possible, but census dates are 10 years apart, with delays before new data is published. • Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) is carried out more regularly than the census (e.g.2015 and 2019) but it quickly becomes out of date. • Maps (current OS or Google maps, and older maps) allow comparison with past land-uses or the extent of housing areas or populations. • Trip Advisor website and blogs and Face Book pages give a useful insight into opinions and may be a safer/less confrontational option to primary data collection, but care in interpretation is needed as they are likely to be unrepresentative of the population as a whole, and may show extreme views so are not reliable. • Other possible sources include blogs, magazines, Geofile, DVDs or websites like Francis Frith or Trip Advisor. Each have their own contribution which could be assessed. Assessment could: • Compare the different secondary sources for their contribution to investigating the research, e.g. assess their bias/validity/ accuracy/ reliability. It could assess where secondary data was most /lease useful. • Consider the difficulties in comparing data sets (e.g. old photos not precisely located or dated). • Consider which sources were the most or least useful for particular aspects of the investigation. All judgements are likely to be partial and tentative given the limited range of primary sources used. No marks if no secondary sources/methods are identified. No marks for secondary data about Coasts or Glaciation unless specifically linked to the research question. Accept any other appropriate response. Level Mark Descriptor 0 No rewardable material. • Shows evidence that fieldwork investigation skills used may not have been Level 1 1–3 fully appropriate or effective for the investigation of the geographical questions/issue. (AO3) • Considers the fieldwork investigation process/data/evidence, with limited relevant connections and/or judgements. (AO3) • Argument about the investigation is simplistic and/or generic. (AO3) • Shows evidence that fieldwork investigation skills used were largely Level 2 4–6 appropriate and effective for the investigation of the geographical questions/issue. (AO3) • Critically considers the fieldwork investigation process/data/evidence in order to make some relevant connections and valid judgements. (AO3) • Argument about the investigation may have unbalanced consideration of factors, but is mostly coherent. (AO3) • Shows evidence that fieldwork investigation skills used were appropriate Level 3 7–9 and effective for the investigation of the geographical questions/issue. (AO3) • Critically considers the fieldwork investigation process/data/evidence in order to make relevant connections and judgements that are supported by evidence. (AO3) • Argument about the investigation includes balanced consideration of factors and is fully developed and coherent. (AO3)
erText: Some candidates still cannot distinguish between primary and secondary data collection, which of course holds back their marks here. Candidates struggled to assess the value of secondary data, and many failed to highlight the different stages where it was used. This latter aspect was addressed a little more than value. Few were able to assess its validity, and instead too many answers were descriptive of the secondary used, and how they had used it, and their only assessment was that it was good. The stages candidates could have discussed in their answers include the following ideas. The Route to Enquiry in the specification mentions secondary data as being used in Stage 2, ‘Contextualising of the field work’ or the planning stage, and it is also likely that centres might use secondary data to help in Stage 6, Analysis and Conclusion section, as well as Stage 7, Critically reflecting on the results. Secondary sources seen included the use of google maps or other online sources to help with the selection of places to collect data, use of maps to select and then find these locations, and to provide a base for the presentation of data spatially. Also, the use of weather maps and bus/train timetables to plan trips. Also, the use of past census data or Index of Multiple Deprivation data to compare locations, and use of photos from the past for comparisons with the present. Some candidates used data collected by previous student cohorts to provide comparisons.

text: 4 Study Figures 4a, 4b, 4c, 4d, 4e and 4f in the Resource Booklet. Sustainability in an urban place involves enhancing the social, economic, and environmental conditions to improve the quality of life and well-being of all current and future residents. Evaluate the extent to which Totnes is a sustainable place to live. (16)
msText: Evaluate the extent to which Totnes is a sustainable place to live. Question number Answer 4 AO1 (4 marks)/AO2 (12 marks) Marking instructions Markers must apply the descriptors in line with the general marking guidance and the qualities outlined in the levels-based mark scheme below. Responses that demonstrate only AO1 without any AO2 should be awarded marks as follows: • Level 1 AO1 performance: 1 mark • Level 2 AO1 performance: 2 marks • Level 3 AO1 performance: 3 marks • Level 4 AO1 performance: 4 marks Indicative content guidance The indicative content below is not prescriptive and candidates are not required to include all of it. Other relevant material not suggested below must also be credited. Relevant points may include: AO1 • Globalisation has created winners and losers for people and physical environments in all parts of the world. • Ethical and environmental concerns about unsustainability have led to increased localism and the awareness of the impacts of a consumer society. • Local groups and NGOs promote local sourcing, including Transition Towns which respond to global concerns by increasing sustainability, which has economic, social and environmental costs and benefits. • Ethical consumption schemes may reduce environmental degradation. • Consideration of the ways economic and social changes have influenced people’s identity. • Places change their functions over time. • International and global influences have shaped places, and lives of people are affected. AO2 • Globalisation has had massive impacts on the environment in terms of waste, pollution, long supply chains and the effects of consumerism. • The lived experience for many people in Totnes includes economic, social and environmental problems, and the community is seeking ways forward to improve the quality of life for its people, but also for the wider world. • Local places have sought strategies to help achieve net zero in terms of encouraging local production and sales and reduce carbon footprints, often on a small scale. • Alongside this regeneration of the local economy and improving social welfare helps to change perceptions of places. • The council, local NGOs and people of Totnes have rebranded the town through the Transition Towns organisation. • The UK government made the commitment to net zero in terms of cutting carbon emissions and local councils like Totnes and NGOs like the Transition Towns movement find strategies to implement this. • The town experiences its own environmental challenges in terms of congestion and importing food, and economic and social problems in terms of low incomes, rising house prices and food insecurity. • These are measured through the different criteria of the IMD data, showing that Totnes is in the 30% lowest deciles for housing, income and income affecting children, and in the 20% most deprived in terms of employment. • Strategies to reduce the unsustainability of the town include Eco homes, local food production and sales, the Reconomy Centre, the Totnes Pound and a community food bank. • Evaluation is likely to consider the extent to which these schemes are successfully addressing global issues. Each of these are small scale schemes and though they do help, they are dependent on volunteers, and some have closed (e.g. the Totnes Pound). Accept any other appropriate response. Level Mark Descriptor 0 No rewardable material. • Demonstrates isolated elements of geographical knowledge and Level 1 1–4 understanding, some of which may be inaccurate or irrelevant. (AO1) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas, making limited and rarely logical connections/relationships, to produce an interpretation with limited relevance and/or support. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to produce an unsupported or generic conclusion, drawn from an argument that is unbalanced or lacks coherence. (AO2) • Limited synthesis of geographical ideas from across the course of study. (AO2) • Demonstrates geographical knowledge and understanding, which is Level 2 5–8 occasionally relevant and may include some inaccuracies. (AO1) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas with limited but logical connections/relationships to produce a partial interpretation that is supported by some evidence but has limited coherence. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to come to a conclusion, partially supported by an unbalanced argument with limited coherence. (AO2) • Argument partially synthesises some geographical ideas from across the course of study, but lacks meaningful connections. (AO2) • Demonstrates geographical knowledge and understanding, which is mostly Level 3 9–12 relevant and accurate. (AO1) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to find some logical and relevant connections/relationships to produce a partial but coherent interpretation that is supported by some evidence. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to come to a conclusion, largely supported by an argument that may be unbalanced or partially coherent. (AO2) • Argument synthesises some geographical ideas from across the course of study, making some meaningful connections. (AO2) • Demonstrates accurate and relevant geographical knowledge and Level 4 13–16 understanding throughout. (AO1) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to find fully logical and relevant connections/relationships to produce a full and coherent interpretation that is supported by evidence. (AO2) • Applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to come to a rational, substantiated conclusion, fully supported by a balanced argument that is drawn together coherently. (AO2) • Argument comprehensively and meaningfully synthesises geographical ideas from across the course of study throughout the response. (AO2)
erText: This question was well answered by most, as long as they gave themselves enough time to complete it. Most candidates were able to use the resource effectively using AO1 knowledge and understanding and were able to link this to sustainability. Less developed responses that didn't go higher than level 2 looked at Totnes' challenges and attempts to alleviate them, without much evaluation other than a summary 'therefore Totnes is/is not sustainable'. Candidates mis-interpreted Figure 4b Unemployment rate, and missed the fact that Totnes has a lower figure. Stronger answers started to evaluate the data from the start. For example, some discussed how ‘unemployment at 2.1% is below the UK average, however jobs are low paid and seasonal’. The IEP was variously seen as good because of health benefits, income, reducing food miles and therefore carbon emissions or ineffective because a large percentage of food has still to be brought in. Stronger responses considered and evaluated both points of view. There was little evidence of ideas from other areas of study or candidates’ own case studies, although one or two candidates referred to Todmorden in relation to transition towns and Mumbai or Chinese cities in respect of the impact of air pollution on health, but not as much as in previous years. The basic evaluation that was given, as mentioned above was given at the end of each paragraph and/or at the end of the answer. Stronger answers offered an evaluative opinion as they discussed each point with an evaluative summary at the end. Most conclusions that were not rushed gave a careful weighing of the relative importance of the pros and cons, the general consensus was that social and economic pros and environmental cons were foremost, but this could change in the future and likely that the social and economic factors would become cons. These responses also considered the extent. Some sat on the fence and said there were pros and cons to each factor, and this tended to hold back their answer to level 3.

msText: Question Explain two ways physical factors influence cultural diversity in one of your Mark number chosen places. Answer 5(c) AO1 (4 marks) (4) For each reason, award 1 mark for a relevant factor and a further 1 mark for expansion, up to a maximum 2 marks each. For example: • A place that is a long distance from an urban place/airport/port may have low ethnic diversity (1) because recent migrants may want to be able to access transport to visit their homes/families overseas (1). • Cities are usually based on flat land/ river crossing points and have ethnic diversity (1) because housing/jobs are focussed there (1). No mark for naming the chosen place. Accept any place as their chosen place. Large places may be over-generalised. Accept any other appropriate response.
erText: Two times two reasons were needed here for this 4-mark question. Some candidates gave one developed idea for 2 marks, and some gave two 1-mark answers. Some were able to achieve between 3-4 marks. The question asked the candidates to explain two ways physical factors influence cultural diversity in one of their chosen places. Problems arose when candidates did not focus on 'physical' and so their responses didn't fit the question. Some candidates seemed to use their fieldwork location which worked well on most occasions, but some struggled, such as those who wrote about Warrington who lacked a physical context for their discussions. Weymouth and other coastal locations were used to discuss cultural diversity in terms of the age of people or their ethnicity. ‘Physical’ is a word AS candidates struggle with and centres are recommended to use it regularly in lessons to help develop confidence in concepts included. Specifically, they need to consider the ways physical geography may or may not influence cultural diversity.

text: (d) Explain how international influences have shaped the characteristics of one of your chosen places. (6) Location of your chosen place:
msText: Explain how international influences have shaped the characteristics of one of Question your chosen places. number Answer 5(d) AO1 (6 marks) Marking instructions Markers must apply the descriptors in line with the general marking guidance and the qualities outlined in the levels-based mark scheme below. Indicative content guidance The indicative content below is not prescriptive and candidates are not required to include all of it. Other relevant material not suggested below must also be credited. Relevant points may include: • Demographic characteristics could be the age or ethnicity, and possibly the gender of the place, and culture might include the different religions or customs of the place. • These are likely to be influenced by the past and present international connections in terms of the people who live in the places now. • Migrant people may cluster with others who speak the same language or share the culture, and find safety, places of worship, shops and restaurants that enrich their lives. • Internationals influences could be the global shift of manufacturing and services to elsewhere in the world, leaving some communities without their traditional employment, so out-migration of working age people and their families may have occurred, affecting the demography of the place. • Allow the idea that there have been minimal international influences on the demographic or cultural characteristics of a place. The reasons for this would need to be developed in a relevant way to go out of level 1. If not linked to the chosen place, the answer is unlikely to go out of level 2. No mark for naming the chosen place, and accept any place. Large places may be over- generalised. Reward specific detail. Allow a range of characteristics, including economic or social characteristics, the built environment and the appearance of the place and its people. Accept any other appropriate response Level Mark Descriptor 0 No rewardable material. • Demonstrates isolated elements of geographical knowledge and Level 1 1–2 understanding, some of which may be inaccurate or irrelevant. (AO1) • Understanding addresses a narrow range of geographical ideas, which lack detail. (AO1) • Demonstrates geographical knowledge and understanding, which is mostly Level 2 3–4 relevant and may include some inaccuracies. (AO1) • Understanding addresses a range of geographical ideas, which are not fully detailed and/or developed. (AO1) • Demonstrates accurate and relevant geographical knowledge and Level 3 5–6 understanding throughout. (AO1) • Understanding addresses a broad range of geographical ideas, which are detailed and fully developed. (AO1)
erText: This 6-mark question invited candidates to explain how international influences have shaped the characteristics of one of their chosen places. As with Q5c, candidates who opted to write about the USA or the UK as a whole lacked the specific detail to move up the level-based mark scheme, and 3 marks on this question tended to be the maximum mark. Choosing a city or ideally a part of a city or town worked more successfully. Some answers were vague, and many lacked specific examples of the characteristics of the places they wrote about. Most answers focused on migration of people and businesses moving in with impacts on culture and diversity or affecting the age structure of a place. Some potentially good answers were limited by generalities, and support would have easily raised the quality of the responses. To gain level 3 marks, it is recommended candidates discuss at least two different international influences, for example migration of people or investment. They should also consider characteristics in terms of economic or social ideas, which could include ethnicity, language or culture as well as the effects on the built environment (mosques, restaurants, TNCs, road signs) to demonstrate the ‘broad range of geographical ideas’ required.

text: (e) Assess why conflicts may occur between stakeholders involved in managing change in diverse places. (12)
msText: Question Assess why conflicts may occur between stakeholders involved in managing change in diverse number places. Answer 5(e) AO1 (3 marks)/AO2 (9 marks) Marking instructions Markers must apply the descriptors in line with the general marking guidance and the qualities outlined in the levels-based mark scheme below. Responses that demonstrate only AO1 without any AO2 should be awarded marks as follows: • Level 1 AO1 performance: 1 mark • Level 2 AO1 performance: 2 marks • Level 3 AO1 performance: 3 marks. Indicative content guidance The indicative content below is not prescriptive and candidates are not required to include all of it. Other relevant material not suggested below must also be credited. Relevant points may include: AO1 • Different stakeholders include local and national government, local businesses and residents as well as a range of specific groups, such as pressure or community groups. • Change could involve the influx of new groups into an area. These could be ethnically different or from different countries but ethnically similar, or asylum seekers rehoused from elsewhere in the country. Another change might be in terms of the age profile with younger or older residents arriving, perhaps over a longer time frame. • Change could involve changes to land use, services, employment and the built environment, including the building of new housing in rural areas or around towns/cities. • Both rural and urban places can be perceived differently by newcomers compared to those who have lived there for longer because of their lived experience. AO2 • Local councils could be argued as the key player in managing rapid cultural change as this may be highly localised; councils provide culturally specific and also more general services in terms of education, health and social services. • In places with rapid cultural change and population movement, there may be challenges in providing some services, especially education, if numbers of children are rapidly rising and special language provision needs to be made. • Tensions or conflicts could occur, unless successful management is able to minimise this. • Places may also experience change in the numbers of elderly people with care needs. This may lead to shortages of staff creating a need for recruitment by businesses and social services, and the National Health Service. • Rural areas may lack provision of services and distances travelled add costs to meet the needs of different groups. • The national government makes decisions about locations of asylum seekers, e.g. Bibby Stockholm moored in Portland, Dorset a rural place where provision of support services will be a challenge. Success could be assessed in terms of managing attitudes to newcomers although there will be jobs and spending locally to benefits some businesses. • Local community groups (ethnic / national groups or religious groups) may help provide community engagement and encourage integration; and build outreach and understanding with the host population, reducing clashes. • Celebrations at special times of the year may generate opportunities for outreach with shared spaces and meals. • Businesses also provide services in areas of rapid cultural change in terms of shops and other services, meeting the needs of the newcomers, but also benefiting from their willingness to work (for those groups allowed to do so)either set up by entrepreneurs from an ethnic group or by others. Judgements will depend on the chosen places, stakeholders and communities. Local councils and community groups might be seen as most significant in terms of managing the process of integration and promoting understanding in areas where there is rapid cultural change. erText: The 12-mark question asked candidates to assess why conflicts may occur between stakeholders involved in managing change in diverse places. Most candidates demonstrated quite strong AO1 understanding, with most identifying a range of stakeholders and the different priorities they have. AO2 application of ideas was also evident using exemplars to develop and exemplify the reasons for the conflicts occurring. However, many answers finished there and did not go on to assess or even mention management. This was why many answers went no higher than level 2 (8 marks).
