erText: Candidates are required to write two 20-mark essays in this paper. The skills required for these extended writing questions are varied and many candidates found these challenging. The command word in these questions is 'evaluate' and answers needed to find logical connections and relationships, produce a full and coherent interpretation supported by evidence from their geographical knowledge and understanding, and then present a balanced argument with a substantiated conclusion. The mark scheme differentiates between 4 levels of performance with many candidates struggling to achieve the top marks at Level 3, and few reaching Level 4. The specification requires centres to teach students about their local place and a contrasting place. This question focused on just one and provided an opportunity for candidates to write about 4 aspects: – past connections, present connections, cultural characteristics and demographic characteristics, before making a judgement about which connections influence their place in which way. Typically, responses focused on ethnicity and age. However, there were some interesting interpretations on the idea of culture (eg shared meanings) which the mark scheme allowed for. Level 2 responses established the way past or present connections influenced either cultural or demographic characteristics. They typically showed realistic and interesting knowledge. The most likely way to achieve level 3 was then to consider both past and present or cultural and demographic characteristics. Typically, that meant reflection on historical economic changes and contrasting it with more recent migration; candidates generally wrote better about past connections than the present. The very best (level 4) often discussed all elements, but there were not many of these, perhaps reflecting candidates being prepared to write about 2 places and offer a comparison (perhaps if they had prepared for previous 9GE02 questions). The best answers were clear about local specific information. It is worth noting that candidates who wrote about very large geographical areas (eg London/ Cornwall) were therefore unlikely to be able to score well. Equally, centres should be discouraged from using generic terms like ‘ethnic enclave’, when the scale does not warrant it. For example, Crawley cannot be considered an ‘ethnic enclave’, particularly given its population is ~70% White British. Finally, a 20-mark ‘Evaluate’ question requires a conclusion. Many candidates have learnt this. Some were often quite superficial, however, for example picking ‘a side of the argument’. Better responses gave a reason or some justification. Better conclusions went further to reflect on whether past or present had a bigger impact on either demographic or cultural characteristics, and the reasons for that in their chosen location. 17 marks were awarded here. The response focuses on Southampton as a whole rather than considering the variations within the area, so there was a potential for largely generic connections to be considered. There is however ongoing evaluation throughout and the response demonstrates clear explanation and links to demographic and cultural impacts. Whilst achieving level 4, the response could have been improved with greater use of supporting evidence which may have been more applicable at a ward rather than city level. The response has however focused on a range of past and present connections. Overall the response applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to find fully logical and relevant connections/relationships. Candidates are encouraged with the large tariff questions to take the time to formulate a plan before they commence writing. This will enable them to consider what pertinent knowledge they should include to address the question as well as to consider the selection of supporting evidence. 4 marks were awarded here. The response has areas of inaccuracy and the candidate has been challenged by their choice of location and would have been better to focus in on either their local or contrasting place. The response touches upon the role of colonialisation but other than this the connections to the question are loose. There is an attempt to link to refugees but this is inaccurately linked to NATO. They have made a connection which fits level 2; however the response on the whole fits the level 1 criteria. There is no attempt at a conclusion either which further limits the candidate’s marks. Overall the candidate applies knowledge and understanding of geographical ideas, making limited and rarely logical connections/relationships. 20-mark ‘Evaluate’ question require a conclusion. Conclusions can be quite superficial, for example picking ‘a side of the argument’. Better responses give a reason or some justification. Question 5 (a)(i)-(iii)

Indicative content guidance The indicative content below is not prescriptive and candidates are not required to include all of it. Other relevant material not suggested below must also be credited. Relevant points may include: AO1 • Countries with higher national incomes and health spending tend to have longer life expectancies. • Over the last century life expectancy has steadily increased across the world. AO2 • There is a positive statistical relationship between healthcare expenditure and life expectancy. In this case it was 99% certainty that the results shown in the table have not occurred by chance. • An increase in health expenditure does not necessarily lead to an increase in life expectancy, for example the USA is an outlier. This is due to citizens spending high amounts on personal health insurance, without necessarily influencing improved life expectancy. • In countries such as South Africa, other issues such as lack of basic sanitation and prevalence of HIV means that the healthcare expenditure is not able to cope with the demand level resulting in lower life expectancies. • Countries such as the UK, provide free healthcare for all (NHS) which increases life expectancy. However there are still significant variations within the UK by county and socio-economic grouping. For example, a seven year difference in life expectancy between professional and unskilled males. • Healthcare expenditure can only go so far in explaining the patterns of life expectancy with other non-medical determinants such as related lifestyle choices being important. These include major risk factors such as smoking, alcohol and unhealthy diets. These could be used to explain life expectancy variations in countries such as the UK and USA. • Japan has one of the highest life expectancies but ranks lower in terms of healthcare expenditure. This can be explained by a low rate of obesity and a unique diet of low consumption of red meat and high consumption of fish and plant based foods when compared to Western countries. Accept any other appropriate response. erText: As with Q03(a)(ii) and Q04(a)(ii), when answering a 6-mark question with a resource, the resource should be used as a stimulus for the response. This question provided a real variety in the quality and focus of the answer. Most candidates could identify a link between health expenditure and life expectancy. However, a significant majority did not comment on the strength of the relationship between the two factors and then didn't incorporate examples or merely offered mirror image statements. Level 1 responses tended to be focused solely on the data, regurgitating the trends amongst the health expenditure and life expectancy whereas others ignored the data or maybe just mentioned one bit of data. Level 2 responses looked for plausible suggestions regarding the ability to provide better healthcare facilities, doctors and medication, as well as education on healthier lifestyles. However, often the reasons were not developed; for example, students mentioned bad diets but did not explain what was bad about them. The strongest answers were able to marry the two elements up, using the data to support points and provide plausible understanding whilst also identifying anomalies such as the USA, which allowed a more reflective consideration of the relationship. Some common responses referred to countries such as the UK providing free healthcare (NHS) whereas in the USA private healthcare is expensive and some people are unable to access the healthcare they need. 6 marks were awarded here. The overall relationship is identified and explained well and the candidate demonstrates accurate knowledge and understanding throughout. Comments on the extent to which the relationship is significant at the 95% level are thoughtful. Overall, the candidate applies their knowledge and understanding to geographical information logically to find relevant connections between stimulus material and the question. 4 marks were awarded here. The candidate has inferred the expected relationship but this is not tackled explicitly. The response has good reasons offered for USA's position and offers intelligent comments about why the relationship may not be accurate in a private healthcare system. The candidate needed to use the information from the question to cover what the relationship is and then why the USA does not fit this. The response has a narrow range so is unable to access level 3 marks. When presented with data candidates should be encouraged to question the outcome or selection of the data as part of their response.

msText: Question Explain why the degree of freedom of speech varies between countries number Answer 5(b) AO1 (8 marks) Marking instructions Markers must apply the descriptors in line with the general marking guidance and the qualities outlined in the levels-based mark scheme below. Indicative content guidance The indicative content below is not prescriptive and candidates are not required to include all of it. Other relevant material not suggested below must also be credited. Relevant points may include: • Freedom of speech is the right for an individual or community to express any opinions without censorship or restraint and without fear of retaliation or legal sanction. • Freedom of speech is a right preserved under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and is granted recognition in law in most nations, however the degree to which it is upheld varies from one country to another. • Countries such as the USA are the most supportive of freedom of speech as it is enshrined in the constitution of the United States through the First Amendment which protects freedom of speech. • Barriers to freedom of speech are common in China where there is heavy government involvement in the media meaning references such as the Tiananmen Square protests and Tibet separatist movements are banned in public and blocked on the internet. Social networking sites such as Facebook and Twitter are also banned through the extensive use of monitoring systems and firewalls. • In Europe the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) guarantees a broad range of human rights including the right to free expression, with any person who feels their rights have been violated can take the case to court. • In the UK citizen’s right to freedom of speech is protected by the ECHR and the Human Rights Act, however there is a wide number of exceptions. In particular, the Communications Act 2003 has been used to restrict what individuals may post on social networks. • A common societal phenomenon is cancel culture by placing limitations on free speech via social or digital ostracisation rather than direct censorship by governments or social media platforms. This is a widespread approach in western countries and normally involves the public withdrawing support from fashion people to try to negatively impact a person’s career prospects. Accept any other appropriate response. erText: The 8-mark essay questions have similar marking criteria to 6-mark essay questions. A 'broad range' of geographical ideas is required, which should be 'detailed and fully developed'. This would mean at least two ideas or themes. Exemplification is almost essential though not specified. In this 8-mark question, candidates were asked to explain why the degree of freedom of speech varies between countries. The majority of answers here included some consideration of the role of government in freedom of speech, in particular North Korea and the censorship provided there. Whilst most answers used named examples of places, many were superficial and showed limited understanding of how the country really impacted on freedom of speech. Stronger answers considered a range of factors affecting it, such as governance, religious and cultural difference, participation in Human Rights conventions, amongst others. Many candidates focused on the restrictive countries but not many explained that citizens of countries such as the UK or USA have a legal right to freedom of speech and that it is part of the US constitution. The use of India in this answer was often executed poorly with regular reference to India being the world’s biggest democracy and therefore speech being free. Centres should consider the discussion of populism and polarising politics which is exactly what we have seen in an increasingly autocratic India where Muslim communities have been actively persecuted and many foreign journalists expelled. Too frequently candidates equated freedom of speech with the right to vote. Understanding the difference in human rights is critical to success in questions where a particular human right is named. It was also noted that a large number of candidates rely on the use of predominantly Muslim countries (eg Saudi Arabia and Afghanistan) to answer questions about variations in human rights. There seems to be an assumption that ‘Sharia Law’ is contrary to all ‘human rights’. Some candidates were able to make a stronger case that women may be prevented from talking to men outside of their family which may restrict their ability to express themselves (although this didn’t go as far as to say they may be restricted from talking to journalists) or go on protests if they don’t have a male relative prepared to escort them. Too many equated other examples of gender inequality with a lack of the right to freedom of expression including being able to drive. Centres should look to ensure that they are teaching material in an informed way so that candidates do not have a generalised understanding of Islam and Muslim countries which risks reinforcing misconceptions. 3 marks were awarded here. The candidate produces a brief response with some basic ideas and just enough explanation to get into level 2. This is shown by an attempt to explain why some authoritarian governments may restrict freedom of speech. Overall, the candidate demonstrates mostly relevant knowledge and understanding. Candidates should consider which reasons they want to lead with to ensure that they are tackling the ‘explain’ command word. 8 marks were awarded here. The response starts with an accurate definition of freedom of speech and the whole response links well to the question focus on freedom of speech. A range of relevant examples are given, looking at freedom of speech both within and between countries. The candidate has a nuanced approach that receives credit. Overall the candidate demonstrates accurate and relevant geographical knowledge and understanding throughout. To achieve level 3 marks, candidates should be including a range of supporting examples and data.

text: (c) Evaluate the view that geopolitical interventions are always controversial. (20)
msText: Evaluate the view that geopolitical interventions are always controversial. Question Answer number 5(c) AO1 (5 marks)/AO2 (15 marks) Marking instructions Markers must apply the descriptors in line with the general marking guidance and the qualities outlined in the levels-based mark scheme below. Responses that demonstrate only AO1 without any AO2 should be awarded marks as follows: • Level 1 AO1 performance: 1 mark • Level 2 AO1 performance: 2 marks • Level 3 AO1 performance: 3 marks. • Level 4 AO1 performance: 4–5 marks. Indicative content guidance The indicative content below is not prescriptive and candidates are not required to include all of it. Other relevant material not suggested below must also be credited. Relevant points may include: AO1 • Geopolitical interventions by countries and international organisations aim to defend human rights or to address development issues. • Interventions can be through development aid, trade embargoes, miltiary aid or indirect/direct military action. • Trade embargoes are a government or international ban that restricts trade with a particular country. This is a political tool used in response to perceived threats to international security or to force the end of human rights abuses. • Interventions can be judged by a range of measures including improvements in areas of human development such as health, education and wealth, or through ‘softer’ data such as freedom of speech, gender equality and the level of democracy. AO2 • Considering how controversial interventions are can be difficult as there is little agreement of how ‘success’ is defined e.g. what should be measured and what progress needs to have been achieved in order to the intervention to be successful. • The use of democracy as a measure of success is seen as a valid strategy. With improvements in freedom of speech, free and fair elections and the provision of economic and political ties as indicators of success. • Often the success of geopolitical interventions is measured by economic growth as it is expected that this drives improvements in health, education, infrastructure and environmental protection. However, geopolitical interventions often overlook the human rights of minority groups such as the Ogoni people in the Niger Delta. • Development aid has a very mixed record of success. It should in theory promote economic and social development, improve healthcare and education, and increase human rights. Examples of less controversial examples include the handling of the Ebola crisis in West Africa or USA support for South Korea allowing it to become a ‘tiger economy’. However this is not always successful as seen in the case of Haiti where despite the high amounts of development aid received, this has had limited impact in driving development. • Development aid tends to be less controversial when directed more at a grass-roots level and focused on education, skills training and healthcare. However, there are concerns that it creates a heavy dependence on donor countries. • Trade embargoes can be viewed as controversial and highly contested with the USA being the dominant user of economic sanctions. With concerns raised regarding the impacts on civilians whilst having little effect on the target country’s government policy. For example, the Cuban embargo of 1962 lasted 40 years, resulting in harm to the health and nutrition of ordinary Cubans. • Military aid has been used over the years due to geopolitical strategic value or to access resource rich areas. The UK provision of military aid to Saudi Arabia has been questioned for fuelling deep rooted disagreements between Sunni Muslims and Shai Muslims, as well as turning a blind eye to Saudi Arabia’s bad record with regards to human rights. • Military interventions tend to be seen as controversial with outcomes judged to be mainly negative. Direct military intervention in Afghanistan, Libya and Syria have demonstrated limited impact in terms of development nor improvement in human rights. • Non-military interventions are less controversial on a whole, with peacekeeping being one of the most effective tools. However, these still rely on countries giving up an element of their national sovereignty to allow the UN peacekeeping mandate. Evaluation The evaluation from candidates will depend upon the examples used and how the candidates have decided to consider and make judgements on controversy. Overall candidates may argue that interventions such as trade embargoes tend to be more controversial, whilst other interventions such as development aid are less controversial as they have a clear track record of success. Accept any other appropriate response. erText: This is a 20-mark extended writing question and candidates were asked to evaluate the view that geopolitical interventions are always controversial. Candidates should look for words such as ‘always’ as they are highlighting that it is not as simple as a yes/no and that debate should be expected and welcomed. Candidates found this question challenging, although a basic balanced approach arguing in favour and against the statement worked well, as well as a substantiated rational conclusion. There was a good range of geopolitical interventions discussed for this response and many candidates drew on a range of different types of interventions, with suitable examples to support. Candidates showed a clear understanding of intervention, with many defining it early on. A range of types of intervention were discussed, although military was by far the most common, as students were able to evaluate its level of controversy. As with the previous 20-mark questions, evaluation was the key thing that held candidates back as responses tended to be descriptive and at times lacked explanation as to why the interventions could be viewed as controversial. Weaker candidates struggled in balancing the different types of geopolitical interventions and tended to describe types of intervention. These candidates focused on just telling the story of different conflicts rather than evaluating why they could be controversial. Level 2 responses tend to lead with generalisations such as the idea that aid provided to Haiti was not controversial because it helped them after a disaster. Case study inaccuracies were common, for example mixing up Syria and Libya and some saying the Iraq invasion of 2003 was led by the UN to assassinate Gaddafi. The more successful responses compared their chosen examples, with most candidates focusing on Iraq, Afghanistan and Yugoslavia. The most successful answers gave a range of interventions from military to aid, embargoes, and development aid; they then evaluated in the conclusion which type was often more controversial than others. However very few appreciated that their viewpoint was democratically based and westernised and did not consider the issue that people of different cultures and backgrounds have a right to self- determination. 18 marks were awarded here. This response starts well with a clear introduction setting out the argument that is going to be made. It covers both military intervention and aid and these are supported with relevant and accurate examples. There is ongoing evaluation and thoughtful comments (eg multilateral aid not tackling corruption). The argument is balanced and coherent with a clear structure. It does not achieve full marks as there are errors in omissions in the knowledge of the candidate. Overall, the response demonstrates accurate and relevant geographical knowledge and understanding throughout. There is a rational, substantiated conclusion, fully supported by a balanced argument that is drawn together coherently. Candidates would do well to spend the time planning their responses before tackling the question set. Here the candidate has made some attempt to do this but it is advised that this is an important part of these 20 mark questions. Question 6 (a)(i)-(iii)

Indicative content guidance The indicative content below is not prescriptive and candidates are not required to include all of it. Other relevant material not suggested below must also be credited. Relevant points may include: AO1 • The percentage of foreign born population varies from country to country depending upon migrant policies, historical ties and engagement with the global economy. • Countries with a higher percentage of foreign born tend historically have tended to be more developed countries, however recent trends seen high levels of foreign born in emerging countries such as the United Arab Emirates. • Cultural diversity of a country varies depending upon factors such as physical isolation and political isolation, as well as the country’s historical identity. AO2 • There is a positive relationship between percentage of foreign born and the cultural diversity score. In this case, the rs value was statistically significant at the 95% level, which suggests that the results shown in the table have not occurred by chance. • There is a very strong relationship between % foreign born in these countries and the cultural diversity score. This was measured by the number of different first languages spoken by the population. • With an increased foreign-born population there is a greater cultural diversity due to a greater range of languages, traditions and assimilation of foods, tastes and dress. • UAE has the second highest cultural diversity scores (0.62) and is ranked first for percentage of foreign born. This can be explained by the high reliance on migrant labour facilitated by the country. These workers are likely to come from many different countries. • South Africa however is ranked first for cultural diversity (0.86) but has a low % of foreign born (ranked 9th). This can be explained by its rich linguistic diversity within the nation itself as there are 11 official languages. • In countries such as Iceland whose physical isolation has been a barrier to migration for many centuries means that cultural diversity scores are low (0.07). This meant the population experienced a strong sense of common identity and cultural hegemony. More recently migration especially of the young population has increased leading to a greater proportion of foreign- born than historically. • In comparison, Singapore is a cultural melting pot of migrants from China, India and Europe. The % of foreign born is high and this has resulted in a higher cultural diversity score than other countries on the table. • Japan has a low cultural diversity score (0.01) and scores low in terms of % foreign-born (rank 11th). This is might be due to its closed migration policy which focuses on maintaining Japanese culture. • The data can be called into question as it may have been selected to create a positive relationship, which may not have been present if different twelve countries had been selected. Allow reasonable explanations for the relationship shown. erText: As with Q03(a)(ii) and Q04(a)(ii), when answering a 6-mark question with a resource, the resource should be used as a stimulus for the response. This answer needed to use information derived from the resource (AO2) and develop ideas using the candidate's own knowledge and ideas (AO1). Many answers achieved one of these assessment objectives, but not both. There were some interesting responses to this question with many good attempts to use the material in the resources to speculate on reasons why countries had different cultural diversity scores. Weaker responses became fixated on the data and this resulted in answers that were highly descriptive, with very little explanation offered for the reasons. Typically, candidates stated the obvious relationships (ie the positive relationship), but better responses then went on to write about the anomalies. In this regard, not many picked up on Iceland’s low cultural diversity score, which could have prompted an interesting comment on Iceland’s pursuit of cultural homogeneity. Better responses recognised the role of government policy in places like Japan and Singapore. The very best candidates also made a link between different factors, but this was not required for a 6-mark ‘Suggest’ question. 6 marks were awarded here. The candidate begins by outlining the general trend and uses two contrasting examples (UAE and Japan) with relevant reasons given. The candidate then considers proportionality which should be commended. The data selected to support arguments is good. Overall the candidate applies knowledge and understanding to geographical information logically to find fully relevant connections/relationships between the stimulus material and the question. When presented with data candidates should be encouraged to question the outcome or selection of the data as part of their response.

text: (b) Explain why political and economic events change the patterns of international migration. (8)
msText: Explain why political and economic events change the pattern of Question international migration number Answer 6(b) AO1 (8 marks) Marking instructions Markers must apply the descriptors in line with the general marking guidance and the qualities outlined in the levels-based mark scheme below. Indicative content guidance The indicative content below is not prescriptive and candidates are not required to include all of it. Other relevant material not suggested below must also be credited. Relevant points may include: • Levels of immigration are closely associated with job opportunities in destination countries. Migrants are able to diversify their income and generate remittances in countries which are economically secure. • Welfare and social protection policies can affect migration patterns. Countries with generous welfare systems can attract higher numbers of migrants. • Political events can initiate migration for example warfare and military occupation. For example, the Ukraine crisis has seen unprecedented numbers of migrants fleeing the conflict zones. • The emergence of migration policies has a direct consequence on migration patterns. These set down laws and procedures that migrants need to adhere to in order to gain access to a country. However, western democracies whilst attempting to restrict immigration are limited by human rights and legal activism. • Globalisation has led to huge inequalities between regions with migratory flows moving mostly from South to North in search of employment and a better quality of life. Accept any other appropriate response. erText: The 8-mark essays have a similar marking criterion to 6-mark essays. A 'broad range' of geographical ideas is required, which should be 'detailed and fully developed'. This would usually mean at least two ideas or themes. Exemplification is a useful route for many candidates, though not essential. In this question, candidates were asked to explain why political and economic events change the pattern of international migration. There were many good answers to this question. Candidates provided many relevant case studies including the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, or the influence of Brexit on different flows of migration into the UK. Weaker responses confused the idea of ‘events’, rather than ‘factors’, or wrote about ‘internal’ rather than ‘international’ migration. The very best responses were able to refer to migration theory, eg relative deprivation, neoliberal economic theory. This was not a necessity for full marks, but provided interesting reading for examiners and suggests some centres are providing in-depth explanation of how migration occurs, rather than just learning factors. Political events used to answer this question tended to be conflict (particularly the Russia- Ukraine war) and Brexit. Students used these to explain but often didn’t really offer much in the way of details about the impacts of these events. The 2008 crash was a popular choice for the economic event. Students generally tried to explain both but often they didn’t explain in enough depth or breadth given this was an 8-mark question – they tended to write about the same as for a 6-mark question (although this may be due to running out of time). The vast majority of candidates were able to explain reasons why political and economic events changes the pattern of immigration. Some responses were imbalanced, insofar as addressing one in more detail than the other, or perhaps not making explicit reference to political and economic events. As in Q6(a)(iv), the most significant barrier to candidates scoring in the upper mark band was the depth and extension of detail in their explanation which occasionally lacked that use or manipulation of specific data which would draw on their own understanding and would, in theory, push the candidates into the upper mark band. 4 marks were awarded here. The candidate has tried to cover both political and economic issues through the use of the Polish migration example and the war in Ukraine. The response in places is too generic to achieve higher marks. Overall the candidate addresses a range of geographical ideas, which are not fully detailed and/or developed. Candidates should consider which reasons they want to lead with to ensure that they are tackling the ‘explain’ command word. 6 marks were awarded here. The candidate's response focuses on two key reasons: war and joining a trade bloc. The example of the trade bloc is applied economically as it mentions less economically developed countries joining such as Poland and then correctly links this to high paying jobs being sought. Syria and Ukraine are valid examples and well used by the candidate in this response. Overall, this level 3 response demonstrates accurate and relevant geographical knowledge and understanding throughout. Make sure you tackle all parts of these short essay questions. Examples should always be included to help you build a fuller answer.

msText: Evaluate the view that westernisation poses the most serious threat to national Question identity in many countries number Answer 6(c) AO1 (5 marks)/AO2 (15 marks) Marking instructions Markers must apply the descriptors in line with the general marking guidance and the qualities outlined in the levels-based mark scheme below. Indicative content guidance The indicative content below is not prescriptive and candidates are not required to include all of it. Other relevant material not suggested below must also be credited. Relevant points may include: • Westernisation is the process by which a country or society adopts the customs and institutions that are said to characterise the Western world. This can happen in many different ways including adopting English instead of native languages, wearing typically Western clothes and a shift in religious belief. • National identity is a person's identity or sense of belonging to one or more states or one or more nations e.g. similar culture, language and traditions. • The spread of Western culture, values, and norms has led to the erosion of traditional cultural practices and beliefs, which are integral to national identity. • Other threats to national identity include globalisation, migration and the increasing ownership of companies and foreign ownership of property, land and businesses. AO2 • The spread of westernised as a result of globalisation leads to openness to foreign values which can erode traditional values and indigenous cultural identity. Evaluate the view that westernisation poses the most serious threat to national Question identity in many countries number Answer • Westernisation is largely driven by retail, food and media, 'westernisation' and is a soft power challenge to national identity by European and North American TNCs. The spread of 'western' culture by TNCs is not a form of global political power play, however, their promotion does naturally bring about a cultural change to places • Rapid economic and income growth are leading to a dramatic shift of Asian diets away from staples and increasingly towards livestock and dairy products, vegetables and fruit, and fats and oils. This has seen diversification of diets away from traditional rice and a move towards a Western diet. This has impacts socially e.g. due to rising obesity but also environmentally. • Property, land and businesses are increasingly owned by non-nationals which impacts national identity. Foreign property investments has pushed up property prices in London, making housing unaffordable for many and non-national ownership of property within the UK is targeted within London, which is seen as an area with a great return on investment. • In some location ethnoscapes or flows of people have resulted in changes to the cultural landscapes, which not only changes the physical landscape but also can result in cultural change as well as making it harder for local residents to live in these areas. • In some locations westernisation is resisted e.g. sales of Valentine's Day cards and associated gifts were targeted by the local government in Kohat, Pakistan, who were worried about the 'western tradition' of honouring a Christian saint. Evaluation • Westernisation has led to the emergence of new hybrid cultures that are unique to each country and that these cultures are not necessarily inferior to traditional cultures. erText: This is a 20-mark extended writing question and candidates were asked to evaluate the view that westernisation poses the most serious threat to national identity in many countries. Although this question was well answered by many candidates, there were as many who struggled to differentiate between globalisation and ‘westernisation’. Many candidates were able to introduce their responses with an effective definition of westernisation and the concept of national identity. There was exemplification of the process of westernisation and how this manifests itself in places at a range of scales and recognising the complexities of both westernisation and national identity. The weakest responses did not consider the impact change had on culture, particularly in regard to national identity. The explanations were often superficial, and quickly moved on to write about migration as an alternative threat. At the lower mark bands candidates merely provide a broad-brush commentary on westernisation without development of the concept of national identity. Middle band responses tended to focus on the role of Western TNCs causing change to Asian diets (eg the role of McDonalds). Centres do need to correct the idea that eating McDonald’s food is evidence of the erosion of local culture or national identity; for example, what is being eaten less, as a result? Too many candidates assumed ‘Food culture’ is synonymous with ‘national identity. Migration was a popular theme as why westernisation wasn’t the only/ main threat to national identity. However, many candidates struggled to go beyond explaining the different ways westernisation is a threat to national identity and as a result did not have any evaluation of that view. At the top levels the responses really drilled down into what westernisation and national identity are from the outset with some decent definitions. Candidates' judgements were detailed and they recognised how westernisation had been not only a threat, but did, in some cases, support the concept of national identity. They also recognised that there are factors other than westernisation which are a threat to national identity. Migration was a common counterargument to westernisation and how cultural assimilation and diffusion can impact on national identity. Thus, their conclusions were plausible with strong use of statistics to support their judgements and conclusions. There were many interesting examples used, for example Barbie dolls banned in Pakistan, French radios playing 40% French music, China’s ‘Great Firewall’. By contrast it was notable that very few candidates commented on themes previously written about in 9GE02 exams, eg internal disunity in Catalonia, or about acquisition of land and or property posing a risk to identity too. Finally, it is worth centres considering whether the French policy of ‘L’exception Culturelle’ can genuinely be used as evidence of a country resisting Western culture. 19 marks were awarded here. The response starts with a detailed definition of westernisation and a hint at national identity. The response overall is well written with good use of geographical terminology throughout. There is a range of ideas supported with accurate examples. There is ongoing evaluation and a valid conclusion. The conclusion could have been extended as it is states that westernisation has taken the largest toll but could have provided a clear rationale for this view for full marks. Overall the candidate applies knowledge and understanding of geographical information/ideas to come to a rational, substantiated conclusion, fully supported by a balanced argument that is drawn together coherently. In an essay like this with several different examples, an evaluative approach which weighs the evidence and makes a summary statement is good practice.

erText: There are two 12-mark ‘assess’ questions in this paper and candidates need to find a route through their answers to consider a range of perspectives in order to find a balanced response. This question was generally tackled sensibly and many candidates were able to access Level 2 or 3 by identifying relevant processes such as the global shift, deindustrialisation, and the rise of global hubs. Stronger responses focused on internal disparities within countries, using examples such as the contrast between the Rust Belt and Silicon Valley in the USA, or between coastal Special Economic Zones and inland provinces in China. Some candidates also explored the North–South divide in the UK, contrasting London’s global connectivity with the economic stagnation of towns like Blackpool or Middlesbrough. These responses often included causal chains linking globalisation to structural economic change, job losses, and widening income gaps. A few high-level responses also considered counterarguments, such as the role of government policy in mitigating inequality, or the fact that globalisation has lifted millions out of poverty in countries like China and India, even as internal disparities have grown. Mid-level responses were often descriptive, focusing on inequality without clearly linking it to globalisation. A common pattern was to describe slums in Mumbai or low wages in Bangladesh without explaining how globalisation processes (eg, TNC outsourcing, trade liberalisation) contributed to these outcomes. Some candidates attempted to compare inequality between countries, which was not the focus of the question. Others discussed global inequality or poverty in general terms, without reference to internal disparities or the mechanisms of globalisation. The candidate presents a thoughtful and well-structured response that demonstrates a solid understanding of how globalisation can increase income inequality within countries. They explore a range of relevant concepts, including the rural–urban divide, the marginalisation of indigenous communities, and the role of remittances. These ideas are supported by appropriate examples, such as the displacement of First Nations communities in Canada due to tar sands development and the linguistic barriers faced by indigenous populations in Australia. This section of the response is particularly perceptive and adds depth to the overall argument. The candidate also references theoretical frameworks, such as Rostow’s model of development, to explain how economic shifts from agriculture to services can exacerbate inequality. This shows a good grasp of geographical theory and its application to real-world contexts. Furthermore, the discussion of remittances from migrant workers in Qatar introduces a counterpoint, suggesting that globalisation can also help reduce poverty in some cases. This balanced approach indicates an awareness of the complexity of the issue. Throughout the essay, the candidate makes ongoing assessments and supported judgements, which are key features of a Level 3 response. However, the final paragraph lacks the depth and clarity needed to fully consolidate the argument. A more developed conclusion that clearly weighs the relative importance of the factors discussed would have strengthened the response. Additionally, while the ideas are strong, the expression is occasionally unclear, and the structure could be improved to enhance the overall coherence. Overall, this is a competent and well-informed response that meets the criteria for Level 3. With a more robust conclusion and clearer communication, it could have reached the top of the level. A mark of 10 is appropriate, reflecting a good understanding of the topic with room for refinement in structure and evaluation. Encourage students to build causal chains (eg, global shift → deindustrialisation → unemployment → income inequality). The candidate begins by suggesting that globalisation can increase income inequality within countries due to advancements in transport technology, such as planes and jets, which they refer to as "shrinking world technology." This has enabled increased migration, leading to a phenomenon known as "brain drain," where well-educated individuals move to areas with better job opportunities and higher incomes. The candidate explains that this leaves behind less educated, lower-income populations with limited opportunities for development, thereby creating significant inequality. While this idea is relevant, it lacks specific place-based context and remains quite general, which limits its effectiveness. In the second paragraph, the response becomes more grounded and moves into Level 2 territory by introducing a specific example involving a transnational corporation (TNC). The candidate discusses Coca- Cola’s operations in India, noting that while the company provides well-paid jobs and economic development for some, it also causes environmental degradation. The pollution of local farmland leads to crop failures, which in turn devastates the livelihoods of local farmers. This creates a stark contrast between those who benefit from TNC employment and those who suffer from its environmental impacts, highlighting a valid form of income inequality. This example is more focused and demonstrates a clearer understanding of how globalisation can have uneven effects within a country. However, the response ends abruptly without offering an overall judgement or conclusion. While two distinct inequalities are discussed—those affecting skilled migrants and local farmers—the analysis lacks depth and cohesion. A more developed evaluation or summary would have strengthened the response. Overall, the answer shows some understanding of the topic and includes a basic example, justifying its placement in Level 2 with a mark of 5. Support students in distinguishing between globalisation as a process and its outcomes, and in evaluating both positive and negative effects.

erText: Most candidates were able to outline the basic premise of Dependency Theory, often referencing the core–periphery model. Stronger responses applied the theory to real-world development patterns, such as unequal trade relationships (eg, Ghana exporting raw cocoa while chocolate is produced in Europe), debt dependency through IMF loans, or the extraction of profits by TNCs from host countries. These responses demonstrated a clear understanding of how dependency is maintained through economic structures and global institutions. Some candidates also referenced the historical roots of dependency in colonialism and how this legacy continues to shape development outcomes. However, many responses remained generic, and a significant number confused Dependency Theory with other models such as Rostow’s Modernisation Theory or Wallerstein’s World Systems Theory. This confusion limited the depth of explanation and application. Some candidates described the theory accurately but failed to apply it to uneven development patterns, which restricted them to mid-level marks. The candidate gives a clear and structured explanation of Dependency Theory using the core–periphery model. They begin by defining the theory and identifying the core as the more developed countries and the periphery as the less developed ones. The response explains that the periphery is exploited by exporting raw materials at low cost to the core. These materials are then processed and manufactured into high-value goods by the core countries, which are sold at a much higher price. This economic relationship means that the core countries develop at a faster rate , while the periphery remains underdeveloped due to their limited ability to add value to their exports. The candidate effectively shows how this dynamic leads to uneven global development , with the periphery trapped in a cycle of dependency. The explanation is concise but hits all the key points: the structure of the global economy , the exploitation of the periphery , and the benefits reaped by the core The use of terminology and the logical flow of ideas demonstrate a secure understanding of the theory. To secure full marks in a 4-mark explain question, aim to include key terminology , a clear chain of reasoning , and, where possible, a real-world example The candidate explains the Dependency Theory by highlighting how less economically developed countries (LICs) are reliant on more developed countries for economic growth. They argue that LICs often produce raw materials that are then exported to richer countries, which use them to generate higher profit margins. The candidate notes that this leaves LICs with minimal profit, preventing them from investing in better machinery or infrastructure. As a result, they remain trapped in a cycle of underdevelopment. This explanation shows a basic understanding of the Dependency Theory, particularly the idea that poorer countries are structurally disadvantaged in the global economy. The candidate makes a valid point about the inability of LICs to reinvest in development due to low returns from raw material exports. However, the response lacks depth and breadth. It does not mention the core- periphery model, historical context (eg colonialism), or provide any specific examples of countries affected by this dynamic. To reach full marks, make sure to include key terms like “core” and “periphery,” and explain how historical exploitation or trade imbalances reinforce dependency. Use real-world examples (eg DRC and cobalt mining) to show how some countries remain stuck exporting low-value goods while others profit. This helps demonstrate a fuller understanding of how the theory explains uneven development.

erText: This question produced a wide range of responses and proved to be a strong differentiator across the cohort. Most candidates were able to identify at least one economic alliance, with the most frequently mentioned being the G7, EU, and USMCA (formerly NAFTA). Stronger responses demonstrated a clear understanding of how these alliances support superpower influence through mechanisms such as trade liberalisation, foreign direct investment (FDI), and the imposition of economic norms and rules. For example, high-level responses often discussed the role of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank (WB) in promoting neoliberal economic policies through Structural Adjustment Programmes (SAPs), with specific examples such as Jamaica or Ghana used to illustrate how these policies extend the influence of core superpowers like the USA. Candidates who reached Level 3 typically structured their responses around two or more alliances and evaluated their effectiveness in supporting global influence. These responses often included comparative analysis, such as contrasting the USA’s influence through the IMF and WTO with China’s use of the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB). Some candidates also considered the limitations of economic alliances, noting that military or cultural power may be more significant in certain contexts. For instance, while the EU wields considerable economic influence, its lack of unified military power was cited as a limiting factor in global geopolitics. Mid-level responses tended to be more descriptive, often explaining what economic alliances are and how they function, but without clearly linking them to the concept of global influence. These responses frequently lacked depth in their examples or failed to evaluate the relative importance of economic alliances compared to other forms of power. Some candidates focused too narrowly on one alliance or conflated economic and military alliances, discussing NATO or military interventions without evaluating their relevance to the question. At the lower end, candidates often misunderstood the term “economic alliance” altogether, interpreting it as any form of international cooperation or simply listing examples of superpowers without linking them to alliances. Some responses drifted into general discussions of what makes a country a superpower, focusing on GDP, military strength, or population size, without addressing the role of alliances. The candidate presents a competent response that demonstrates a reasonable level of knowledge and understanding of the topic. The answer engages with the question and attempts to explore the implications of global disconnection, particularly in relation to economic and trade organisations. The candidate identifies a valid point about the potential limitations faced by countries that are excluded from global trade networks, suggesting that this could hinder access to markets and reduce economic competitiveness. This shows an awareness of the broader consequences of isolation in a globalised economy. However, the response contains a factual inaccuracy—specifically, the claim that China is disconnected from economic and trade organisations. This undermines the strength of the argument, as China is in fact a key player in global trade and a member of major institutions such as the World Trade Organisation (WTO). While this error detracts from the overall credibility of the response, the candidate does attempt to present a counterargument, which is a positive feature. They acknowledge that some countries may pursue self-sufficiency or benefit from protectionist policies, indicating an understanding that global integration is not universally beneficial. The use of supporting evidence is present but limited in scope and precision. The examples provided are not fully developed, and the analysis lacks depth. There is some attempt at assessment, but it remains superficial and does not fully explore the implications or weigh the relative importance of the factors discussed. The structure of the response is clear enough to follow, but the argument would benefit from more detailed evidence and a stronger evaluative conclusion. Overall, this is a solid Level 2 response that meets the criteria for a mid-range mark. It shows some understanding and attempts analysis, but inaccuracies and limited evaluation prevent it from reaching Level 3. A mark of 6 out of 12 is appropriate, reflecting a response with potential but in need of refinement in both content and clarity. To strengthen your evaluation in a 12-mark question, make sure you clearly weigh up both sides of the argument This response uses good examples like the USA’s involvement in NAFTA and China’s economic ties with Africa to support the view that economic alliances help superpowers maintain global influence. However, to reach the top level, you should develop your counter-argument more fully For example, explore how soft power (like cultural influence or media) or military alliances (like NATO) might be more important than economic ones. A well-balanced conclusion that reflects on the relative importance of different types of power will help you access the higher mark bands. The candidate presents a well-informed and structured response that demonstrates a clear understanding of the multifaceted nature of global influence. The answer is rooted in accurate and relevant knowledge, with appropriate use of geographical terminology that enhances the clarity and academic tone of the argument. The candidate effectively explores the role of economic factors in shaping global influence, while also acknowledging the significance of non-economic dimensions such as military alliances and cultural connections. This broadens the scope of the response and reflects a more holistic grasp of the topic. A key strength of the response lies in its attempt to balance perspectives. The candidate introduces counterarguments that consider how soft power—through cultural exports or diplomatic ties—can rival or even outweigh economic dominance in certain contexts. This is supported by examples, though the evidence could be more specific and detailed to fully substantiate the claims. The inclusion of a perceptive point about the reduction in national sovereignty adds analytical depth, showing an awareness of the trade-offs that come with global integration and influence. This insight elevates the response beyond simple description and into more evaluative territory. The ongoing assessment throughout the essay is another positive feature, as the candidate does not simply list factors but attempts to weigh their relative importance. However, the final paragraph lacks the synthesis needed to fully consolidate the argument. A more developed conclusion that clearly draws together the economic and non-economic strands of the discussion would have strengthened the overall coherence and impact of the response. Additionally, while the ideas are strong, the answer would benefit from more precise supporting evidence—such as named countries, organisations, or case studies—to reinforce key points and push the response further into the top of Level 3. Overall, this is a competent and thoughtful response that meets the criteria for Level 3. It demonstrates a good understanding of the topic, with some insightful analysis and a balanced approach. With a more robust conclusion and stronger use of evidence, it could have achieved a higher mark. A score of 10 is appropriate, reflecting a solid performance with clear potential for refinement. To reach the top level in a 12-mark “assess” question, make sure your argument is well- balanced and clearly structured A strong summary should weigh up the relative importance of economic alliances compared to other forms of power, rather than simply listing them. This helps demonstrate a sustained and evaluative judgement , which is key for accessing the highest marks

erText: This question was generally well answered, with most candidates able to identify a plausible way in which the street art festival contributed to reimaging. Stronger responses linked the visual transformation of the area to improved perceptions, increased footfall, or the attraction of investment and tourism. These candidates often made reference to the multiplier effect or the idea of place rebranding, showing a clear understanding of how cultural initiatives can contribute to regeneration. For example, some candidates noted that the vibrant colours and artistic expression could change the narrative of a formerly industrial or neglected space, making it more appealing to both residents and visitors. Some responses tended to describe the image or mention that the area “looked better” without explaining how this contributed to reimaging. A number of candidates missed the opportunity to link the visual change to economic or social outcomes. Weaker responses simply described the artwork or the festival without making any connection to the concept of reimaging or regeneration. The candidate suggests that the street art festival has helped reimage the area by “raising the aesthetics” of the surroundings. They go on to explain that this visual improvement may “result in the interest of businesses to locate/set up here,” which would in turn “provide some jobs” and help “prevent it from entering a spiral of decline.” This shows a clear understanding of how cultural regeneration can lead to economic revitalisation. The response earns full marks by establishing a logical chain of reasoning : improved aesthetics (AO2) → increased business interest → job creation → prevention of decline. Each point is clearly stated and builds on the previous one. For 3-mark “suggest” questions, aim to build a clear chain of reasoning. Start with a visible change (eg improved aesthetics), then explain the knock-on effects (eg attracting investment, creating jobs). erText: This is a 6-mark, AO1 and AO2 question based on a resource. The weighting is equal with AO1 being awarded 3 marks and AO2, also 3 marks. This question was generally well understood, and many candidates were able to access Level 2 or 3 by identifying reasons why reimaging may not be effective for all stakeholders. Stronger responses explored the role of lived experience, historical memory, and socio-economic realities in shaping perceptions. For example, some candidates noted that long-term residents may remain sceptical of cosmetic changes if underlying issues such as poverty, crime, or unemployment persist. Others highlighted that reimaging may benefit certain groups (eg, tourists, investors) while excluding or alienating others (eg, low-income residents, ethnic minorities). Level 3 responses typically included two well-developed reasons, supported by examples or references to stakeholder perspectives. These responses demonstrated a nuanced understanding of how perception is shaped by both media and lived experience. Some candidates referenced gentrification and the idea that reimaging can mask deeper inequalities. Mid-level responses tended to identify valid reasons but lacked development or failed to consider multiple viewpoints. Weaker responses were generic, often stating that “some people might not like it” without explaining why or linking to the concept of perception. The candidate presents a thoughtful and focused response that demonstrates a good understanding of the challenges involved in changing people’s perceptions of place. The answer identifies different social groups—such as older residents and those who have lived in the area for a long time—whose views may be more resistant to change. This shows an awareness of how personal experience, age, and attachment to place can shape and solidify perceptions over time. The candidate’s focus on these demographic factors adds depth to the analysis and reflects a nuanced understanding of the social dimensions of place-making. The response is clearly rooted in the negative aspects of perception, discussing why certain groups may hold onto outdated or negative views of a place despite regeneration or rebranding efforts. This focus is valid and well-explained, but it limits the breadth of the response. A more balanced answer might have explored how perceptions can also be positively influenced, or how younger or newer residents might respond differently. Additionally, the response would have been strengthened by introducing a contrasting example from another place—perhaps one where perceptions have successfully shifted over time—to provide comparative insight and demonstrate wider contextual understanding. The use of terminology is appropriate, and the structure of the response is clear and logical. However, the analysis could be further developed with more specific examples or case studies to support the points made. Despite these limitations, the response meets the criteria for Level 3, showing accurate knowledge, relevant application, and some analytical depth. A mark of 5 out of 6 is appropriate, reflecting a strong answer with minor areas for improvement in balance and evidence. To score well in 6-mark “suggest why” questions, make sure you consider multiple perspectives and develop your points fully This response does a good job of explaining how lived experience and stakeholder perspectives (eg long-term residents vs. developers) can shape perceptions of reimaging strategies. To improve further, try to structure your answer clearly , with each paragraph focusing on a distinct reason. You should also aim to link your ideas back to the question —for example, by explicitly stating why these factors mean that reimaging may not succeed in changing perceptions. Including specific examples (like Bristol or a named regeneration project) can also help demonstrate application and boost your marks. The candidate provides a response that demonstrates a basic but relevant understanding of the factors that can influence the success of place rebranding. Two distinct ideas are presented: one relating to the physical transformation of a place and the other concerning community engagement. The first point is reasonably well-developed, showing awareness that visible improvements to the built environment—such as new infrastructure or amenities—can help shift public perception and attract new investment or visitors. This reflects a sound grasp of how tangible changes can contribute to rebranding efforts. The second point, which touches on the importance of community engagement, is less clearly explained. While the candidate correctly identifies that involving local residents is important, the reasoning behind this is underdeveloped. There is little exploration of how community buy-in can foster a sense of ownership, reduce resistance to change, or ensure that rebranding efforts reflect the needs and identity of the local population. The response is structured and coherent, and the ideas presented are relevant to the question. However, the lack of detailed explanation and absence of supporting examples limit the overall effectiveness of the answer. There is no reference to specific places or case studies, which could have helped to illustrate the points more vividly and demonstrate wider contextual understanding. Overall, this is a solid Level 2 response. It shows some understanding and attempts to engage with the question, but the second idea is not fully developed. A mark of 3 out of 6 is appropriate. For 6-mark “suggest why” questions, it’s important to go beyond surface-level ideas and develop your reasoning. This response identifies that negative past experiences and a disengaged community can prevent reimaging strategies from changing perceptions. These are valid points, but to improve further, the candidate could expand on how and why these factors matter—eg how long-term stigma or lack of community involvement undermines regeneration efforts. Try to structure your answer clearly, with each paragraph focusing on a different reason, and use phrases like “this means that…” or “as a result…” to show the cause-and-effect relationship. Including a specific example (like Bristol or a named reimaging project) can also help demonstrate application and boost your marks.

erText: This question was generally well answered, with most candidates able to identify at least one group and explain the nature of the inequality they face. Stronger responses identified two or more groups — such as the elderly, young people, migrants, or low-income families — and explained how factors like poor transport, limited healthcare, lack of employment, or digital exclusion contribute to inequality. For example, some candidates discussed how elderly residents in rural Cornwall may struggle to access healthcare services, while young people may leave due to a lack of job opportunities or affordable housing. Level 3 responses provided clear explanations with specific examples, often drawing on case studies such as Cumbria, Northumberland, or Devon. Some candidates also referenced second- home ownership and its impact on housing affordability for local residents. Mid-level responses tended to identify relevant groups but lacked depth in their explanations or failed to link the inequality to specific rural characteristics. Weaker responses were generic, often stating that “rural areas have fewer services” without identifying who is affected or why. The candidate presents a well-structured and thoughtful response that demonstrates a clear understanding of the reasons why some groups experience inequalities in rural places. The answer identifies two distinct and relevant ideas: the marginalisation of ethnic minority groups and the economic challenges faced by local businesses in rural areas such as Cornwall. These points are explained with reasonable clarity and show an awareness of both social and economic dimensions of rural inequality. The discussion of ethnic minorities is particularly strong in its recognition of how cultural perceptions and potential discrimination can affect inclusion and opportunity in rural communities. This reflects a good grasp of social geography and the role of identity in shaping lived experience. The second point, focusing on financial struggles and lack of government support, is also valid and relevant. It highlights the structural challenges rural areas face, such as limited accessibility and reduced funding, which can lead to business closures and reduced quality of life. However, the response could be further strengthened by including specific place-based examples to support the points made. While Cornwall is mentioned, the answer would benefit from more detailed reference to particular towns, statistics, or case studies (eg Redruth, St Ives, or data on rural deprivation). Additionally, identifying specific social groups —such as elderly residents, young people, or seasonal workers—would add clarity and depth to the analysis. Overall, this is a strong Level 3 response. It demonstrates accurate knowledge and understanding, with some analysis and application. A mark of 5 out of 6 is appropriate. To reach the top level in a 6-mark “explain” question, you need to clearly identify specific groups, link them to types of inequality, and explain how rural characteristics contribute to these outcomes. This response does a good job of highlighting ethnic minorities and local business owners as vulnerable groups, and it explains how rural isolation, lack of funding, and distance from services can lead to economic and social disadvantage. The candidate provides a basic response that demonstrates limited understanding of the question’s focus. While the answer is nominally based in Cornwall, it lacks any specific local examples or case study detail to support the points made. This weakens the geographical grounding of the response and limits its ability to show applied knowledge. The candidate makes general statements about people moving, but does not identify specific groups—such as retirees, second-home owners, or young people leaving for urban areas—which would have added clarity and depth. As a result, the response remains vague and lacks the precision needed for higher-level marks. Several ideas are repeated or closely mirrored, which reduces the range of points covered and suggests a lack of development in the argument. Furthermore, the response begins to drift away from the question’s focus, shifting into a broader discussion of rural–urban differences rather than staying centred on the specific dynamics of population change in Cornwall. This lack of focus, combined with the absence of detailed explanation or evidence, keeps the response firmly within Level 1. Overall, this is a limited answer that shows some awareness of the topic but lacks the specificity, structure, and development required for a higher level. A mark of 2 out of 6 is appropriate. To move beyond Level 1 in a 6-mark “explain” question, you need to provide a clear explanation of why specific groups experience inequalities in rural places, supported by relevant examples or concepts. To improve, the candidate should structure their answer using a framework like DWAGES (Demographic, Wealth, Access, Gender, Education, Services), and clearly explain how rural characteristics—such as isolation, limited services, or employment opportunities—create disadvantage for particular groups.

erText: This question was generally well received, and many candidates demonstrated a solid understanding of the challenges involved in delivering regeneration that satisfies a diverse range of stakeholders. Stronger responses recognised that regeneration is not a neutral process — it often involves trade-offs between economic growth, social equity, and environmental sustainability. These candidates identified a wide range of stakeholders, including local residents (both long-term and new), local businesses, developers, local and national government, environmental groups, and community organisations. They evaluated how regeneration projects may benefit some of these groups while marginalising or excluding others. Level 4 responses were characterised by sustained evaluation, a clear structure, and well- integrated case studies. These candidates often explored tensions between top-down and bottom-up approaches, short-term vs. long-term impacts, and economic vs. social priorities. For example, many discussed the London Docklands regeneration, highlighting how the area was transformed into a global financial hub but at the cost of displacing working-class communities and eroding local identity. Others used Stratford (post-2012 Olympics) to show how regeneration brought investment and infrastructure but also led to rising rents and gentrification. Some candidates contrasted these with more inclusive, community-led projects such as Grampound in Cornwall, where local consultation and shared ownership helped meet a broader range of stakeholder needs. The best responses also considered the role of scale and governance. For instance, they evaluated how national-scale projects like HS2 or the Northern Powerhouse may prioritise economic connectivity over local social needs, while smaller-scale initiatives may be more responsive but limited in impact. Some candidates also reflected on the concept of “legacy” — questioning whether regeneration projects deliver sustained benefits or merely short-term gains for select groups. Mid-level responses tended to focus on one or two stakeholders or case studies, often describing the regeneration process without evaluating its effectiveness. These responses sometimes conflated regeneration with general urban change or failed to differentiate between types of stakeholders. Weaker responses were descriptive, lacked structure, or made generalised claims about regeneration being “good” or “bad” without reference to specific examples or stakeholder perspectives. The candidate presents a case study-led response that demonstrates a sound understanding of the challenges involved in meeting the needs of all stakeholders in regeneration projects. The structure is clear and logical, with each paragraph focused on a specific example, including the London Olympic Park , HS2 , and the Eden Project in Cornwall These case studies are relevant and used to explore a range of stakeholder perspectives, such as local residents, national government, developers, and environmental groups. The response is largely descriptive , with each case study used to illustrate how different groups were affected by regeneration. There are some evaluative comments at the end of each paragraph, which show an attempt to assess the extent to which stakeholder needs were met. For example, the Olympic Park example highlights the tension between economic success and local displacement, while the Eden Project is used to show how environmental and local concerns can conflict with economic development. However, the evaluation remains partial and surface-level The response tends to describe what happened rather than fully analyse the implications or explore the complexity of stakeholder conflict. There is limited synthesis between examples, and the argument would benefit from a clearer overarching judgement. The conclusion makes a valid point about the short-term versus long-term impacts of regeneration, but this is not fully developed or linked back to the examples in a meaningful way. To move into Level 4, the candidate would need to: Provide deeper evaluation of stakeholder perspectives, including more critical reflection on trade- offs and unintended consequences. Compare and contrast the case studies to draw broader conclusions. Develop a more decisive and synthesised conclusion that clearly addresses the question. Overall, this is a competent and well-informed response that meets the criteria for Level 3. It demonstrates good use of case studies and some evaluation, but lacks the depth and synthesis required for the top band. A mark of 12 out of 20 is appropriate. To move into the higher mark bands, students should go beyond description by clearly weighing up how different stakeholder needs conflict or align, and by offering a more balanced argument. Stronger answers also link examples more precisely to the question, showing how specific groups benefit or lose out. Always aim to explore both sides and justify your conclusion with clear reasoning. The candidate presents a well-developed and evaluative response that demonstrates a strong understanding of the challenges involved in meeting the needs of all stakeholders in regeneration projects. The essay is clearly structured, with a logical progression of ideas and a consistent focus on the question throughout. The response draws on a good range of case studies , including Liverpool One , Sunderland’s Foundation of Light , and Haworth , each used to explore different stakeholder perspectives. The Liverpool One example is particularly effective in showing how regeneration can benefit both high-income consumers and lower-income families through employment opportunities. The Sunderland case adds a valuable social and cultural dimension, highlighting how regeneration can support education and community identity. The Haworth example introduces the idea of generational conflict and differing stakeholder priorities, which adds nuance to the discussion. There is ongoing evaluation throughout the essay, with the candidate weighing up the extent to which regeneration projects can be inclusive. The use of geographical terminology such as “gentrification,” “circular economy,” and “stakeholder conflict” is appropriate and enhances the tone of the response. The candidate also shows an awareness of the subjective nature of success , noting that different groups may define success in different ways. To move further into the top of Level 4, the response could be improved by: Synthesising the examples more explicitly, drawing comparisons between them to highlight patterns or contrasts in stakeholder outcomes. Developing the conclusion to more clearly consolidate the argument and offer a final judgement. Including more critical reflection on long-term impacts or unintended consequences of regeneration, particularly in relation to displacement or sustainability. Overall, this is a confident and well-informed response that meets the criteria for Level 4. It demonstrates detailed knowledge, effective use of case studies, and a clear evaluative approach. A mark of 16 out of 20 is appropriate. To reach the top level in a 20-mark “evaluate” question, you need to present a well- structured, balanced argument that considers a range of stakeholder perspectives and uses detailed case study evidence.
